roles.description: Teach academic, social, and life skills to preschool-aged students with learning, emotional, or physical disabilities. Includes teachers who specialize and work with students who are blind or have visual impairments; students who are deaf or have hearing impairments; and students with intellectual disabilities.

tasks.label: Develop or implement strategies to meet the needs of students with a variety of disabilities.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Developing individualized strategies for a child on the caseload: reviewing IEP goals and evaluation data, selecting accommodations (visual schedules, AAC/PECS boards, adapted scissors, seating/positioning equipment), and physically preparing the classroom materials and environment (laminating symbol cards, arranging a quiet corner, setting up a stander or adapted chair) in a public preschool/early-childhood special education classroom.

Implementing differentiated strategies during group instruction (circle time, centers, small group) in a self-contained or inclusive preschool classroom with 8-15 three-to-five-year-olds of mixed disabilities: cueing with picture symbols, signing to a child who is deaf, hand-under-hand tactile guidance for a child with visual impairment, redirecting wandering children, handing out and swapping manipulatives, all while managing a paraprofessional and the group's pace.

Implementing 1:1 skill instruction with physical prompting for a child with motor or intellectual disability: hand-over-hand shaping of pencil grasp, cutting, spoon use, handwashing or dressing; transferring and positioning the child in adaptive equipment; fading prompts and recording trial-by-trial data, in the classroom or therapy corner.

Implementing behavior support strategies during dysregulation for a child with emotional/behavioral disability: reading early signs, offering a sensory break, physically blocking or redirecting a child who is eloping, hitting, or throwing, moving other children to safety, and returning the child to the activity, in a preschool classroom or hallway.

Implementing and modeling strategies outside the school building: an early-childhood home visit or a community childcare/Head Start placement where the teacher adapts the found environment, demonstrates the prompting or communication strategy with the child, and coaches the caregiver or aide.

sources.title: Robot Mediated Instruction for learning disability using QTrobot
sources.claim: QTrobot, the leading commercial special-needs-education social robot, sits on a table and delivers speech/gesture/facial-expression content to a seated student while an instructor drives the session from a tablet app; it provides no physical prompting, material handling, or strategy development.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-mediated instruction of students with learning disability. It is the closest deployed analogue to 'implementing strategies', but it covers only a scripted content-delivery sub-step under human operation, so it does not transfer to whole-task completion.

sources.title: How the RoboKind Robots for Autism and SEL Make an Impact
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo/Veda/Carver robots are deployed in US special education classrooms as facilitator-run tools that help special educators teach social-emotional and communication modules; the educator remains the one who selects and runs the strategy.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: delivering an SEL/social-skills curriculum to autistic students. It substantiates only a supplementary lesson-delivery role beside a teacher, not development or implementation of individualized strategies across a variety of disabilities.

sources.title: Socially Assistive Robotic Instruction for Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder
sources.claim: Research-grade socially assistive robots for autism instruction deliver structured lessons through a tablet interface, and their effectiveness for academic learning is still being tested in preliminary studies.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered academic instruction to children with autism. It shows the state of the art is tablet-mediated scripted lessons of unproven effectiveness, which cannot substitute for a teacher implementing individualized strategies.

sources.developer: LuxAI / Luxembourg Institute of Health / University of Birmingham
sources.title: LuxAI, Luxembourg Institute of Health, and University of Birmingham launch the first large-scale study of at-home, robot-led early development support for autistic children with QTrobot
sources.claim: Robot-led early development support for autistic children in the home is still at the stage of a first large-scale trial, not demonstrated deployment; results are not expected until the end of 2026.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: at-home robot-led early autism intervention. It is an ongoing trial rather than a demonstrated capability, so it cannot substantiate completion of home-based strategy implementation.

tasks.label: Communicate nonverbally with children to provide them with comfort, encouragement, or positive reinforcement.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Maintain accurate and complete student records as required by laws, district policies, or administrative regulations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Teach socially acceptable behavior, employing techniques such as behavior modification or positive reinforcement.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-group or whole-class circle-time instruction in an inclusive preschool special education classroom: teacher models and rehearses sharing, turn-taking, hand-raising and greetings with 6-12 children of mixed abilities, delivering labeled verbal praise and a sticker/token when a child performs the target behavior.

In-the-moment teaching during free play or centers: a child grabs a toy, pushes, or screams; the teacher interrupts, prompts a replacement behavior ('ask for a turn'), and immediately reinforces the appropriate response, using differential reinforcement and planned ignoring of the problem behavior.

One-on-one structured teaching (discrete-trial or naturalistic milieu) with a minimally verbal child with autism or an intellectual disability: teacher presents a social instruction, uses a prompt hierarchy including gestural and hand-over-hand physical guidance, and delivers an immediate reinforcer, running many trials and recording data.

Implementing an individualized behavior intervention plan for a child with severe challenging behavior (aggression, elopement, self-injury): running a token economy or first/then contingency, prompting functional communication, collecting ABC data, and keeping the child and peers safe during escalation.

Teaching self-regulation and social routines across the daily schedule and outside the classroom - transitions with visual schedules, calm-down corner use, lining up, playground and cafeteria behavior - and reinforcing generalization of the taught behavior in those less controlled settings.

tasks.label: Attend to children's basic needs by feeding them, dressing them, or changing their diapers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Diaper/pull-up change for a 3-5 year old with disabilities (e.g., cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, developmental delay) on a classroom changing table: lifting/positioning a child who may be stiff, floppy, or resistant, removing soiled clothing, cleaning skin, applying barrier cream, fastening a fresh diaper, redressing, disposing of waste, sanitizing the surface, hand hygiene, and logging the change.

Toileting support and accident cleanup in the classroom bathroom: transferring the child onto an adapted toilet or potty chair, physical support during voiding, wiping, pulling up clothing, washing the child's hands, and changing wet/soiled clothes into spare garments while managing the child's distress.

Snack/lunch feeding for a child with oral-motor difficulty, dysphagia risk, tube-plus-oral feeding, or sensory/behavioral feeding refusal: positioning the child, presenting modified-texture food on a spoon at the child's pace, cueing chewing and swallowing, watching for coughing/aspiration, redirecting refusal, wiping face and hands, and recording intake.

Snack/lunch feeding for a child whose disability is purely motor (e.g., arthrogryposis, SMA, spastic quadriplegia) who chews and swallows safely and can activate a switch: teacher sets up food and feeds bite by bite at a classroom table alongside peers.

Dressing/undressing at arrival, departure, outdoor play, or nap: coats, hats, mittens, boots and shoes with laces/velcro, plus donning/doffing AFO braces, splints, or adaptive garments on a wiggling or spastic child who may need hand-over-hand prompting to participate.

The same personal-care duties (diaper change, feeding, dressing) performed outside the classroom: during a home visit for a home-based early-intervention preschool program, or on a community outing/field trip where the changing surface, bathroom, and furniture are whatever is available.

sources.system: EmPRISE robot-assisted feeding system (ADA arm, 'Feel the Bite')
sources.title: Robotic system feeds people with severe mobility limitations
sources.claim: Cornell's EmPRISE lab built an autonomous robot-assisted feeding system with real-time mouth tracking and force-aware inside-mouth bite transfer; it fed 13 adults with conditions such as spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy and MS across a lab, a medical center and one home. It is a research demonstration performing bite transfer only, with users directing it via tongue/mouth interaction.
sources.transferJustification: Same physical act as the feeding instances (delivering food to the mouth of a person who cannot self-feed), but demonstrated only with cooperative adults who direct the robot, and covering only bite acquisition/transfer, not positioning, swallow-safety monitoring, refusal management, or cleanup.

sources.title: Obi Robotic Feeding Device | School Health
sources.claim: Obi is a commercially sold, FDA-listed Class 1 robotic feeding device distributed to US schools; it automatically scoops from four compartments and delivers food to a caregiver-taught mouth position, triggered by the diner's accessibility switch. Vendor states diners must be able to operate it and to chew and swallow unassisted.

sources.developer: DESIN LLC (deployed at Paxson Elementary School, Missoula MT)
sources.title: 'Freedom!' Obi robot gives student with cerebral palsy independence
sources.claim: A school-aged student with cerebral palsy began using an Obi robotic feeder to eat his meals during lunchtime with classmates at a Montana public elementary school, i.e., the device is in real use inside a school food-service setting in place of an adult feeding the child.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the feeding portion of this task, in a school; the user is 9 rather than preschool age, and the device only substitutes for adult spoon-feeding when the child can chew, swallow and trigger a switch.

sources.system: Force-Modulated Visual Policy (FMVP) dressing system on a Sawyer arm
sources.developer: Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute (Hao, Wang, Held, Erickson)
sources.title: Force-Modulated Visual Policy for Robot-Assisted Dressing with Arm Motions
sources.claim: State-of-the-art autonomous robot-assisted dressing puts one sleeve of a long-sleeved garment onto a seated adult's arm in a lab; with the garment already grasped by the robot, it covered on average 85% of the arm length over 264 trials with 12 healthy adults aged 21-39, taking up to 80 seconds per trial with documented failures.
sources.transferJustification: Closest published work to the dressing instance; it shows that even the sub-step of sleeving one cooperative adult arm in a lab is not yet reliable, and it excludes coats, shoes, braces and wiggling toddlers.

sources.system: Compliant gripper for robot-assisted trouser dressing/undressing
sources.title: Development of a Compliant Gripper for Safe Robot-Assisted Trouser Dressing-Undressing
sources.claim: Robot-assisted trouser dressing/undressing remains at the component-development stage: work reported in December 2025 is a new compliant gripper design, with prior systems reaching roughly 73% success and starting from the assumption that the robot already holds the clothing.
sources.transferJustification: Covers the lower-body dressing/undressing needed for diapering and toileting instances; shows the capability is pre-prototype even for cooperative adult recipients.

tasks.label: Teach basic skills, such as color, shape, number and letter recognition, personal hygiene, or social skills, to preschool students with special needs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-group or whole-class instruction (circle time, centers) in a preschool special education or inclusive classroom: teacher teaches color, shape, number and letter recognition using manipulatives, flashcards, songs and books, handing out and positioning materials, prompting responses, redirecting off-task behavior, and taking data on 4-8 children with mixed disabilities.

One-to-one or dyad structured instruction at a table or resource-room station on a specific pre-academic target (matching colors, identifying shapes, counting, letter-sound recognition) with a child who can attend to a tabletop or screen task, using massed trials, prompting and reinforcement, and recording trial-by-trial progress toward IEP goals.

Teaching personal hygiene and self-care routines in the classroom bathroom, sink and cubby area: handwashing, toileting and toilet training, nose blowing, dressing and coat/shoe management, delivered with modeling, visual schedules, hand-over-hand physical prompting and prompt fading, plus handling accidents and clean-up.

Teaching social skills during play and routines: greetings, turn-taking, sharing, requesting, waiting, joining peers and resolving conflicts, coached in real time on the rug or playground, including physical redirection, co-regulation of a dysregulated child, and arranging peer-mediated practice.

Instruction adapted for sensory or motor disabilities: pre-braille/tactile symbol and object-cue work with a blind child, sign language and listening/spoken-language work with a deaf or hard-of-hearing child, or teaching basic concepts to a nonverbal child with significant intellectual and physical disabilities who needs positioning, adaptive equipment and AAC.

Home-based or community early-intervention session in a family's home: teaching the child basic concepts and self-help skills within family routines using whatever materials are present, coaching the parent to continue the strategies, and documenting progress.

sources.system: Kiwi socially assistive robot (USC Interaction Lab)
sources.developer: University of Southern California (Maja Mataric lab)
sources.title: Children with autism could benefit from USC assistive robot
sources.claim: Kiwi, an autonomous socially assistive robot paired with a touchscreen, ran near-daily instructional sessions on number/math concepts with 17 children aged 3-7 with autism in their own homes for a month, personalizing instruction and feedback in real time; all participants improved on the taught math skills and 92% on social skills.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered instruction of early number concepts to preschool-aged children with autism. It maps onto the pre-academic (number/shape/letter recognition) portion of this task with the same age range and population, at a fixed station comparable to a resource-room teaching table.

sources.title: Can Milo the Robot Help Autistic Children Connect? | Edutopia
sources.claim: Milo, a commercially sold social robot used in US special-education programs for autism social-skills lessons, is deployed as a teacher/therapist tool: an adult facilitator brings the student to the robot, prompts the student, and manages the session.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-mediated teaching of greetings and social behaviors to children with autism in a school. It is the closest commercial system to this task's social-skills instruction, but the cited deployment shows a human facilitator delivering and supervising the lesson.

sources.system: Robot-assisted therapy platform (Babes-Bolyai University randomized trials)
sources.title: Efficacy and effectiveness of robot-assisted therapy for autism spectrum disorder: From lab to reality | Science Robotics
sources.claim: Two randomized clinical trials of robot-assisted therapy for young autistic children (mean ages 4.4 and 5.9) targeting joint attention, imitation and turn-taking found outcomes equivalent to conventional therapist-delivered treatment; the robot mediates sessions run by clinicians rather than replacing them.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-assisted teaching of joint attention, imitation and turn-taking to preschool-aged autistic children, i.e. the social-skills component of this task. Robot autonomy within the clinician-led sessions is not established, so the item cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.title: Haksh-E: The robot who mentors good handwashing - Amma.org
sources.claim: Haksh-E/Pepe is a wall-mounted social robot installed near school washrooms that autonomously recognizes handwashing actions and gives feedback to encourage proper handwashing technique among primary-school children; it prompts and nudges but provides no physical assistance or hand-over-hand guidance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered hygiene instruction to children in a school. It is the nearest system to the personal-hygiene component, but it only verbally coaches typically developing school-age children and cannot deliver the physical prompting, fading, toileting support or clean-up preschoolers with disabilities require.

sources.title: Robot teachers invade Chinese kindergartens
sources.claim: Keeko, an autonomous wheeled classroom robot, has been deployed in Chinese kindergartens as a teaching assistant that tells stories and poses logic problems to groups of children, with the human teacher running the classroom.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robot delivering group learning content to preschool-aged children in a classroom. It marks the current ceiling for group instruction: spoken content delivery only, with no material handling, prompting hierarchy or behavior support of the kind special-needs preschool teaching requires.

tasks.label: Develop individual educational plans (IEPs) designed to promote students' educational, physical, or social development.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Prepare classrooms with a variety of materials or resources for children to explore, manipulate, or use in learning activities or imaginative play.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Before the school day, the teacher sets up learning centers in the preschool special-ed classroom per that day's plan: puts out blocks, puzzles, board books, dolls, sorting bears and art supplies on low tables and open shelves, arranges chairs and rugs, and labels bins with picture cards. Items are heterogeneous, small, and often already partly out of place from the previous day.

Prepares sensory, tactile and adapted materials: scoops rice/beans/water into sensory bins, mixes and portions play dough, cuts and laminates picture-symbol cards, assembles visual schedules and choice boards, prepares textured/braille-labeled objects and high-contrast items for children with visual impairments, and lays out paint, glue and paper for a messy art activity.

Resets and replenishes materials during and between activity rotations: gathers scattered toys and manipulatives off the floor and shelves them by category, swaps one center's materials for the next activity, wipes and sanitizes mouthed toys, and restocks paper, wipes and snack supplies — all while children are in the room or during a short transition window.

Sets up child-specific adaptive equipment per IEP at individual work stations: positions an adapted chair with lateral supports and footrest, clamps a slant board or tray, mounts an AAC device or switch on a wheelchair tray, plugs in and tests a switch-activated toy, and places weighted or textured supports at the right child's seat.

Prepares a gross-motor or outdoor space controlled by the school: sets out tunnels, balance beams, therapy balls, ride-on toys and mats in the gym or fenced playground for a motor-skills session, then collects and stores them afterward.

Itinerant/home-based service: packs and lays out a kit of toys, books, manipulatives and adapted materials in a family's living room or a community childcare room the teacher does not control, adapting the setup to whatever furniture, floor space and clutter is found there.

sources.title: Meet Sparrow: Amazon's new item-picking robot - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm autonomously detects, picks and places individual items of widely varying shape — including plush toys, socks and DVDs — in fulfillment-center workcells, though it cannot handle the full item catalog.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: warehouse piece-picking/kitting. Objects (plush toys, small consumer goods) and precision (grasp from a tote, place into a destination bin) match selecting classroom toys and manipulatives into activity kits when the items are presented at a fixtured station.

sources.title: Staples deploys RightHand Robotics tech in its fulfillment centers | Supply Chain Dive
sources.claim: RightHand Robotics' RightPick piece-picking cells are commercially deployed across Staples' North American fulfillment centers, autonomously picking individual varied items into order totes.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: order-fulfillment piece picking of school/office goods (Staples SKUs: markers, paper, small supplies) into totes — the same grasp-and-place operation as assembling trays of classroom supplies at a purpose-built station.

sources.title: Introducing Chef+: Our Most Advanced Meal Assembly Robot Yet | Chef Robotics
sources.claim: Chef Robotics' AI-enabled arms are deployed on food-manufacturing lines, autonomously portioning scoopable material and placing discrete items into trays and packages at production rates.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: scooping and depositing bulk granular material into trays on a line — mechanically equivalent to filling sensory bins with rice/beans and portioning dough or art media into containers at a fixtured station.

sources.title: Inbolt and FANUC Pioneer Robots that Think and Act on the Fly at Moving Assembly Line Speeds | Automate.org
sources.claim: Vision-guided FANUC robot cells with Inbolt AI perform screwdriving and part insertion on parts without indexing fixtures, a commercially released industrial assembly capability.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: industrial assembly (fastening and insertion) in a robotic cell. Mounting a switch, clamp or slant board onto a fixtured tray involves comparable part handling, alignment tolerance and fastening in a purpose-built setting.

sources.title: Swisslog Healthcare Partners with Diligent Robotics to Enhance Hospital Logistics
sources.claim: Diligent Robotics' Moxi mobile manipulator is deployed in more than 25 ... performing autonomous point-to-point supply and pharmacy deliveries, but its work is fetch-and-deliver transport rather than arranging assorted materials across a room.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous material transport inside an institutional human facility. It establishes E2 navigation and delivery, but not the diverse fine placement and arrangement of loose materials this task requires.

sources.title: Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid passes 100,000-tote milestone in live GXO implementation
sources.claim: Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid has moved over 100,000 ... a GXO warehouse, doing repetitive tote pick/place between AMRs, conveyors and floor locations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: humanoid material handling in a structured facility. Shows deployed institutional mobile manipulation is limited to uniform totes at defined stations, not heterogeneous small-object arrangement.

sources.title: Helix 02 Bedroom Tidy | Figure
sources.claim: Figure's Helix-02 humanoids autonomously reset a bedroom (hanging clothes, putting away objects, making a bed) in a company demonstration; this is a staged single-take demo, not a deployment with measured reliability.
sources.transferJustification: Closest match to whole-room material setup/reset, but as a vendor demo in a staged room it does not establish worker-quality reliability, throughput, or handling of a classroom's item variety.

sources.title: A VLA with Open-World Generalization | Physical Intelligence
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's pi-0.5 model drives a mobile manipulator to perform multi-step tidying (dishes, laundry, drawer organizing) in homes it has never seen, as a research result with partial success rates.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: open-world tidying and object placement. It is the strongest evidence for unstructured-setting material handling, but remains a research demonstration without worker-level reliability.

tasks.label: Meet with parents or guardians to discuss their children's progress, advise them on using community resources, or teach skills for dealing with students' impairments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial
