automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Observe and evaluate students' performance, behavior, social development, and physical health.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Read books to entire classes or to small groups.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Confer with parents, administrators, testing specialists, social workers, or other professionals to develop individual education plans (IEPs).

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Instruct and monitor students in the use and care of equipment or materials to prevent injuries and damage.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-group fine-motor/art or table activity in a self-contained or inclusive preschool special education classroom: the teacher demonstrates safe use of scissors, glue sticks, markers, stampers and blocks, provides hand-over-hand guidance to 3-5 year olds with autism, developmental delay or motor impairments, physically blocks unsafe acts (poking, throwing, mouthing small parts), and teaches putting materials back, capping markers and wiping the table.

Adaptive and assistive equipment instruction: teaching an individual child to use and care for a walker/gait trainer, adaptive seating, hearing aids and FM system, glasses, braille/tactile materials, or an AAC speech device or tablet - correct handling, charging/storage, cleaning, not dropping or chewing the device - with the teacher positioned to guard against falls and equipment damage.

Gross-motor time in the school gym or fenced preschool playground: instructing children with disabilities in safe use of climbers, slides, swings, sensory swings, trikes and balance equipment, spotting and physically intercepting unsafe use, and teaching them to return equipment to bins at the end of the period.

Self-care and routine materials in the classroom: teaching safe use and care of eating utensils and cups, toothbrushes, soap and paper towels, sensory bins, water and sand tables and cleanup sponges; watching for choking, spilling and mouthing hazards among several children at once and stepping in physically when needed.

Off-site or non-school settings: community outing, bus/van boarding, or a home visit in which the teacher instructs the child (and often the family) in safe use and care of equipment - stroller/wheelchair straps, communication device on the bus, playground or store carts - in a setting whose layout and contents are taken as found.

sources.developer: NUWA Robotics (study by Jürgensen & Kubina, Penn State)
sources.title: Socially Assistive Robotic Instruction for Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder
sources.claim: The most advanced socially assistive robots used with young children with autism deliver scripted lessons through a tablet interface in a research setting; they do not handle classroom materials, demonstrate tool use, or supervise children for safety.
sources.transferJustification: Closest robotic analogue to instructing preschool-aged children with disabilities; cited to show that even purpose-built special-education robots deliver verbal/tablet lessons only, with no manipulation of equipment or physical injury prevention, so capability does not transfer to this task.

sources.system: NAO / Milo / QTrobot special education packages
sources.title: Special Education Robots for SPED | RobotLAB
sources.claim: Commercially sold special-education robots are marketed as engagement and social-skills tools operated alongside a teacher, not as systems that supervise children's use of physical equipment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is robot-assisted social/academic instruction in SPED classrooms; cited to show the commercial state of the art is stationary conversational tabletop robots that cannot monitor a group or physically intervene, so it does not carry over to equipment-safety instruction and monitoring.

sources.system: Haptic robotic pen-skill trainer (Phantom-type haptic arm)
sources.developer: University of Leeds researchers (PLOS ONE study)
sources.title: Robot Guided 'Pen Skill' Training in Children with Motor Difficulties
sources.claim: Haptic robotic arms can physically guide a seated child's hand through pen strokes in a controlled research setup, but the device is a fixed desktop trainer requiring adult setup and shows no transfer beyond the device.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is physical hand-over-hand guidance in tool use, a component of this task; cited because it is the strongest physical-guidance evidence, yet it is a fixtured single-purpose trainer that neither monitors for unsafe use nor teaches care of materials, so it cannot complete the whole instance.

sources.system: Vevo nursery robot with sensor system
sources.developer: Global Bridge Holdings / Social Solutions (with Gunma University)
sources.title: Day care facilities test robots as high-tech solution to alleviate staffing shortages - The Japan Times
sources.claim: Robotic/sensor systems piloted in institutional childcare settings monitor children for records and staffing support; they do not instruct children or physically prevent injuries.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is monitoring young children in an institution-controlled childcare facility; cited to show that deployed child-monitoring robots only sense and log, providing no instruction, no manipulation and no physical intervention, so they cannot substitute for supervision that prevents injuries.

sources.system: Realbotix M-Series humanoid 'Sally' with Optio AI assistant
sources.developer: Realbotix / Salamanca City Central School District
sources.title: New York School District Introduces Robotic Humanoid Teaching Assistant
sources.claim: The first announced US school-district humanoid deployment is a stationary conversational AI assistant for 11th- and 12th-grade classrooms under full district oversight, with no manipulation or supervisory role.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is robotic teaching assistance in a school; cited as the frontier of school robot deployment as of mid-2026 - a conversational, non-mobile, non-manipulating system for older students - showing no system exists that could supervise preschoolers' equipment use.

tasks.label: Establish and enforce rules for behavior and procedures for maintaining order among students.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Circle time / whole-group instruction in a preschool special education classroom: teacher states and reviews class rules with visual supports and songs, cues 6-12 children with autism, developmental delays or sensory impairments to sit on the rug, keep hands to self and take turns, gives proximity cues, and physically guides or re-seats children who wander, flop or grab peers' materials.

Transitions and routines (arrival, clean-up, lining up, hand-washing, toileting, moving to the gym or playground): teacher runs the procedure using timers, transition songs and picture schedules, uses least-to-most prompting including hand-over-hand physical prompts, blocks doorway elopement, and keeps the group together and safe while paraprofessionals handle individual children.

Free play / learning centers: teacher supervises children spread across several centers, enforces sharing and safety rules, intervenes in toy conflicts by separating children and removing thrown or unsafe objects, delivers token/reinforcement systems, and models replacement behaviors for nonverbal or limited-verbal students.

Implementing an individual behavior intervention plan for a child with severe challenging behavior (aggression, biting, self-injury, elopement, dropping to the floor): antecedent strategies, prompting, escort to a calm-down space, protective physical intervention/CPI-trained holds when safety requires, incident documentation and ABC data collection.

Establishing the rules and procedures themselves at the start of the year or after a team meeting: designing classroom expectations and visual rule charts, arranging furniture and materials to prevent problem behavior, setting up reinforcement systems, explicitly teaching each routine, and training paraprofessionals to apply them consistently.

Outdoor playground and off-campus outings (bus ride, community field trip, walk to the park): enforcing safety rules on equipment, keeping a line or buddy system, counting and tracking children in an open, uncontrolled space, and intercepting a child who runs toward a street or parking lot.

sources.title: How a Robot Named Milo Helps Special Needs Students in Pendleton, SC Learn
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo is a commercially deployed, facially expressive tabletop humanoid used in K-12 special education to deliver scripted social-emotional lessons (greetings, emotions, turn-taking, coping) to a student, with an educator/facilitator present; it has no mobility or manipulation for supervising or redirecting a group of children.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered social-skills instruction to students with disabilities. It does not transfer to establishing and enforcing classroom rules: Milo works one-to-one from a pre-authored curriculum with a human facilitator managing the child's behavior, is stationary, and cannot monitor a whole preschool group, arbitrate conflicts, or physically redirect a child.

sources.system: NAO and other classroom social robots (research deployments)
sources.title: Surprising Performances of Students with Autism in Classroom with NAO Robot
sources.claim: Reviews of social robots placed in real school settings for children with autism report feasibility of presence but persistent difficulty achieving long-term, highly autonomous robot-child interaction, and no demonstrated superiority over human teachers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous child-robot interaction in classrooms. It is the closest capability to autonomously managing preschool behavior, and the literature reports that sustained autonomous interaction is not yet achieved, so it cannot substantiate autonomous rule enforcement among a group.

sources.title: Day care facilities test robots as high-tech solution to alleviate staffing shortages
sources.claim: Nursery/childcare robots deployed in Japan (Vevo, Global Bridge Holdings with Gunma University) are monitoring and record-keeping aids — sensing attendance, movement, temperature and sleep — not systems that direct children's behavior or maintain order.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic supervision of young children in a childcare facility. It shows the deployed state of the art is passive monitoring; nothing in it substantiates prompting, redirecting, or physically intervening with preschoolers to maintain order.

tasks.label: Provide assistive devices, supportive technology, or assistance accessing facilities, such as restrooms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Restroom/diapering assistance in the preschool classroom bathroom: teacher walks or carries a 3-5 year old with a disability to the toilet or changing table, manages clothing, provides physical support on an adapted toilet seat, wipes and cleans, handles accidents, then dresses the child and supports handwashing. Child may resist, be non-ambulatory, or have low trunk control.

Transfers, positioning equipment and moving about the building: lifting a child from wheelchair to floor mat, cube chair, stander or gait trainer, fastening straps and harnesses, then escorting or pushing the child through doors, ramps, hallways, to the playground, gym, cafeteria or bus loading area with hands-on physical support.

Providing and setting up supportive technology: retrieving a charged speech-generating device/tablet or switch, mounting or aligning it on a wheelchair tray or table within the child's reach and gaze, opening the right vocabulary page, positioning an eye-gaze or switch-activated toy, and troubleshooting during a classroom activity.

Handing out and fitting small adaptive materials during table-top or circle-time activities: adapted scissors, pencil grips, slant boards, non-slip mats, adapted spoons, weighted vest, seating the child in an adapted chair with a foot support, and adjusting fit while the child works.

Sensory-device management for children who are deaf/hard-of-hearing or blind/low-vision: placing hearing aids or cochlear implant processors on the child, checking batteries and clipping on an FM/DM receiver, putting on glasses, and handing over braille/tactile materials and a cane, checking placement throughout the day.

sources.developer: RIKEN and Sumitomo Riko Company Limited
sources.title: The strong robot with the gentle touch | RIKEN
sources.claim: ROBEAR, the best-known robot for lifting a person from a bed into a ..., was an experimental research prototype from RIKEN/Sumitomo Riko, not a deployed product, and lifted a cooperative adult under caregiver guidance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: transferring a person between bed and wheelchair. It is the closest demonstrated analogue to lifting/transferring a child between wheelchair, mat and adapted equipment; its prototype status and reliance on an operator show the transfer does not carry over to unsupervised classroom transfers of children.

sources.developer: WHILL, Inc. (with Envoy Air / American Airlines)
sources.title: WHILL and Envoy Deploy Autonomous Service at U.S. Airports
sources.claim: WHILL's autonomous wheelchairs are commercially deployed in US airport terminals, driving passengers to their gates without a human pusher.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: moving a seated person through a building. It shows autonomous transport of a rider in a controlled facility, but the rider boards, sits and disembarks unaided, so it does not carry over to escorting a preschooler who needs lifting, strapping and constant supervision.

sources.system: WHILL autonomous wheelchairs at Detroit Metropolitan Airport
sources.developer: WHILL / Unifi / Wayne County Airport Authority
sources.title: Wayne County Airport Authority partners with Unifi to bring autonomous wheelchairs to DTW
sources.claim: Airport operators describe the autonomous wheelchairs as serving self-sufficient riders while human staff continue to handle passengers needing hands-on care.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assisted mobility in a facility. It establishes the boundary of current autonomy — hands-on assistance is explicitly still reserved for human staff — which is exactly the kind of assistance a preschool special-ed teacher provides.

sources.title: Serve Robotics to Acquire Diligent Robotics, Expanding Physical AI Platform Beyond the Sidewalk
sources.claim: Moxi is an autonomous hospital delivery robot deployed at scale in US hospitals, fetching and delivering supplies, medications and lab samples for staff, with no patient-contact caregiving.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fetching and delivering items in a structured institutional building. It covers only the transport sub-step of providing a device; Moxi does not position equipment on a person or interact physically with patients, so it cannot complete the whole instance.

sources.title: Bimanual Robot-Assisted Dressing: A Spherical Coordinate-Based Strategy for Tight-Fitting Garments
sources.claim: Robot-assisted dressing — the manipulation class needed to put garments, vests or devices onto a person — remains an active laboratory research topic, with methods still being developed for cooperative, largely stationary adult subjects.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: placing clothing/equipment on a human body. It is the nearest analogue to dressing a child after toileting or fitting a vest/hearing aid; its lab-only status and assumption of a still, cooperative adult show it does not transfer to preschoolers.

sources.title: Robots for Humanity: In-Home Deployment of Stretch RE2 (ACM/IEEE HRI 2024 Companion)
sources.claim: The assistive mobile manipulator most used with severely disabled people in homes, Hello Robot's Stretch, is operated by the user through a teleoperation interface rather than performing assistive tasks autonomously.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fetching and handing objects to a person with disabilities. It is the closest analogue to providing an assistive device to a child, but the demonstrated capability is teleoperated, so it cannot support a positive judgment.

tasks.label: Monitor teachers or teacher assistants to ensure adherence to special education program requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Administer tests to help determine children's developmental levels, needs, or potential.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Ongoing curriculum-based/observational assessment in the preschool special education classroom (AEPS, Teaching Strategies GOLD, Brigance IED-III): during centers and routines the teacher sets out materials to elicit target skills (stack blocks, name pictures, cut with scissors, follow directions), observes 3-5 year olds with mixed disabilities, and scores items while other children and aides move around the room.

One-to-one standardized norm-referenced developmental evaluation for eligibility/IEP (BDI-3, DAYC-2, Bayley-4) in a quiet school assessment room: teacher opens a kit of manipulatives (rings, blocks, crayons, pegboard, picture easel), builds rapport, presents items in order, re-presents or adapts for refusal, judges partial credit, establishes basals/ceilings, and records scores.

Pre-academic, concept, and speech-language screening with picture cards, objects, and pointing responses, done at a table in the classroom corner or a small room; child may respond by pointing, gesture, or AAC device, and the teacher must distinguish a wrong answer from inattention or motor difficulty.

Adapted administration for a child with sensory or motor disability: tactile/braille-readiness materials for a blind child, sign-language or visually presented administration for a deaf child, switch or eye-gaze access, plus physical positioning, hand-over-hand support, and modified item scoring.

Progress-monitoring probes on IEP goals embedded in the school day: short discrete-trial or curriculum probes with flashcards, objects, or manipulatives, run between activities with a child who may resist, elope, or need behavioral supports, with correct/incorrect data logged on a sheet or tablet.

sources.developer: The Chinese University of Hong Kong with NEC Hong Kong Limited
sources.title: Development and evaluation of robotic detection technology for assessing autism (Front. Psychiatry 16:1636560)
sources.claim: The HUMANE social robot autonomously narrated stories to 119 children aged 3-6 in a university treatment room designed for child assessment while its computer-vision system detected atypical eye gaze and ... and prompted the child; detection reached about 0.80 sensitivity/specificity against ADOS-2. A human experimenter seated and instructed the child, and the output is one contributing signal toward an autism diagnosis, not a multi-domain developmental profile.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: a robot-led screening session with preschool-aged children (3-6), including autistic children, in a room used for child assessment. It is the closest analogue to test administration, but it presents no standardized manipulative items, yields no developmental levels or domain scores, and a human seats and instructs the child, so it does not carry over to whole test administration.

sources.system: JIBO social robot as GFTA-3 test administrator (UCLA pilot)
sources.developer: UCLA (Johnson, Martin, Quintero, Bailey, Alwan); robot by Jibo Inc.
sources.title: Can Social Robots Effectively Elicit Curiosity in STEM Topics from K-1 Students During Oral Assessments?
sources.claim: A JIBO social robot delivered the GFTA-3 sounds-in-sentences protocol to kindergarten and first-grade children in an empty office at a school site by playing pre-recorded prompt audio; a human assessor sat in and intervened whenever the child could not proceed, and researchers scored all responses manually afterward.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: administering a standardized speech assessment to young children in a school room. It is directly on point, but the robot only replayed scripted prompt audio with a human assessor backstopping it and human researchers scoring, so it cannot substantiate autonomous whole-test administration.

sources.system: Pepper robot with RoboMate MMSE protocol
sources.developer: IRCCS Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza with Behaviour Labs (B-Labs), Italy
sources.title: Assessing Feasibility of Cognitive Impairment Testing Using Social Robotic Technology Augmented with Affective Computing and Emotional State Detection Systems (Biomimetics 8(6):475)
sources.claim: A Pepper robot administered the Mini-Mental State Examination to older patients in an Italian geriatric study, with sessions run under the supervision of a psychologist and managed through a remote RoboMate dashboard.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot administration of a standardized cognitive test. Transfer fails: examinees are cooperative verbal adults in a clinic, a psychologist supervises each session, and no manipulative kit is handled, whereas preschool developmental testing requires presenting and manipulating physical items with a 3-5 year old with disabilities.

sources.system: QTrobot for Schools / special needs education
sources.title: QTrobot for special needs education - LuxAI S.A.
sources.claim: QTrobot for special needs education is a commercial robot used in schools and therapy centres, with 300+ pre-built educational units, structured prompting, and automated session reporting; the delivered package includes an educator tablet used to control the robot during sessions, so a human educator drives and supervises the session.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: delivering structured discrete-trial style units and progress data to children with autism in special education classrooms. It is the most mature classroom system for this population, but it is operated from an educator tablet, so it cannot substantiate autonomous administration of assessment probes.

tasks.label: Teach students personal development skills, such as goal setting, independence, or self-advocacy.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Embedded instruction in daily self-help/independence routines in an early childhood special education (ECSE) classroom: arrival and coat/backpack removal, handwashing, snack (spoon, cup, opening containers), toileting, cleanup. Teacher uses graduated guidance and hand-over-hand physical prompting with 3-5 year olds who have motor, intellectual, or multiple disabilities, then fades prompts across weeks and records IEP data.

Small-group/circle-time instruction on independence and choice-making with 6-10 preschoolers with mixed disabilities: following a picture schedule, choosing a center, doing a classroom 'job', transitioning, waiting and turn taking, cleaning up. Teacher must simultaneously manage attention, elopement, tantrums, and sensory needs while individualizing prompts.

One-to-one structured teaching of self-advocacy/communication targets at a teaching table or in-context: requesting help, asking for a break, refusing appropriately, indicating needs using speech, sign, picture exchange, or an AAC device. Includes error correction, reinforcement, prompt fading, trial-by-trial data collection, and generalization checks with a nonverbal or minimally verbal child.

Teaching simple goal setting and self-monitoring: 'first-then' boards, token/sticker charts tied to a personal goal, reviewing with the child what they accomplished, praising effort and persistence, and helping the child notice their own progress. Embedded in play and academic activities in the classroom.

Teaching and generalizing independence/self-advocacy outside the classroom: playground, hallway, cafeteria, a community outing, or an early intervention/itinerant home visit where the teacher coaches the family in the child's own home or childcare setting. Layout and materials vary site to site; pets, siblings, and clutter are present.

sources.title: LuxAI - Award winning social robots for autism and special needs education
sources.claim: QTrobot (LuxAI) is a commercially sold social robot used in special needs education and schools, but is positioned as a teacher/therapist-operated assistive tool for increasing engagement rather than an autonomous instructor that runs a child's program.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered social-emotional lessons to children with disabilities in schools. It is the closest commercial analogue to teaching personal-development skills, but the source describes a supervised tool used alongside the educator, not a system that completes the instruction.

sources.date: 2016 (case study); program in district use through 2024-2025
sources.title: IESD Case Study: Children on the Autism Spectrum Show Improvement with Robots4Autism (Spartanburg)
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo robot delivers a scripted robots4autism social-emotional curriculum (calm down, conversational, emotional, situational modules) to students with ASD in US school districts, paired with a student iPad and run with an adult facilitator who reviews the data.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: teaching self-regulation and social skills to students with disabilities in a school. Transfer is limited: Milo runs fixed curriculum modules on a screen-plus-robot script with a facilitator present, and does not individualize IEP targets, physically prompt, or manage a preschool group.

sources.title: Improving social skills in children with ASD using a long-term, in-home social robot | Science Robotics
sources.claim: An autonomous social robot (Jibo platform) was deployed in family homes for 30 days, 30 minutes per day, delivering therapy-derived games that improved social communication skills of children with ASD aged 6-12, with a family member present throughout.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robot-delivered social-skill instruction to children with disabilities in an unstructured home. It is the strongest autonomy evidence found, but the children were school-aged, a caregiver co-participated and set up each session, and the robot supplemented rather than replaced the human interventionist.

sources.developer: Babes-Bolyai University / DREAM consortium (David, Vanderborght et al.)
sources.title: Efficacy and effectiveness of robot-assisted therapy for autism spectrum disorder: From lab to reality | Science Robotics
sources.claim: Randomized clinical trials of in-clinic robot-assisted therapy with preschool-aged autistic children (mean age 4.4 years) achieved outcomes equivalent to conventional treatment with higher engagement; the underlying DREAM framework operates the robot under supervised autonomy with the therapist in control of the session.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: structured teaching of joint attention, imitation and turn-taking to preschool-aged children with disabilities in a clinic. It bears on 1:1 skill instruction, but the therapy is therapist-delivered with the robot as an element of the session, so it does not show a robot completing the teaching.

sources.system: DREAM / DREAM Lite supervised-autonomy robot therapy system
sources.developer: DREAM consortium (Senft, Thill, Vanderborght, Vernon et al.)
sources.title: DREAM Lite: Simplifying Robot Assisted Therapy for ASD (arXiv)
sources.claim: The DREAM robot-enhanced therapy architecture explicitly keeps the robot under the therapist's control, targeting only enough autonomy to reduce therapist workload rather than independent delivery of the intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as the RCT above; this source establishes the autonomy status of the platform used, showing continuous human supervision and control rather than the limited-intervention autonomy required here.

tasks.label: Employ special educational strategies or techniques during instruction to improve the development of sensory- and perceptual-motor skills, language, cognition, or memory.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: 1:1 or small-group language/communication instruction in a self-contained or inclusive preschool special-ed classroom: teacher sits at a table with a 3-5 year old, presents objects and picture cards, runs PECS exchanges or AAC device modeling, uses milieu teaching (mand-model, time delay, expansion), physically hands over/blocks materials, delivers reinforcers, and adjusts prompt level as the child responds or escapes.

Fine-motor / perceptual-motor instruction: teacher positions the child, sets up pegboards, beads, scissors, crayons, puzzles or sensory bins, and uses a graduated prompting hierarchy including hand-over-hand and hand-under-hand physical guidance, fading physical support to partial and shadow prompts across trials, while managing mouthing, throwing, and refusal behavior.

Cognition/memory instruction: discrete-trial or naturalistic teaching of matching, sorting, sequencing, object permanence, and short memory games with concrete manipulatives; teacher presents arrays, blocks errors, uses errorless correction, collects trial-by-trial data, and adapts the strategy within the session based on the child's performance.

Gross-motor and sensory-integration activity in the classroom or school motor room/gym: obstacle courses, balance and ball work, movement songs, swings, brushing or deep-pressure input; teacher physically supports and spots the child, adjusts the equipment, and keeps a group of children with varied motor and behavioral needs safe.

Whole-group circle time (6-10 children with mixed disabilities plus aides): songs with movement, visual schedules, choral responding, individualized prompts and reinforcement delivered on the fly, redirecting children who elope or dysregulate while continuing the lesson.

Itinerant or specialized-disability instruction, e.g., an ECSE teacher working in a community childcare room or family home, or teaching a child who is blind or deaf: tactile/pre-braille exploration, tactile signing and hand-under-hand guidance, adapted play routines, checks of hearing devices, in a setting the teacher does not control.

sources.title: QTrobot for special needs education - LuxAI S.A.
sources.claim: QTrobot is a commercially sold social robot used in special-needs schools and therapy centers; it ships with an educator tablet used to control the robot and a learner tablet for the child, and is positioned as a supplement to the teacher rather than a substitute, with the educator present throughout the session. It has no functional hands and does not manipulate teaching materials.
sources.transferJustification: Directly on task: a robot delivering language, cognition and social-skill educational units to preschool-aged children with disabilities. Cited to show the mode of use (educator-controlled adjunct, no material handling), which bears on whole-instance completion.

sources.system: iCub humanoid robot, robot-assisted training (RAT) protocol
sources.developer: Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia / clinical research team (ISRCTN15341724)
sources.title: Enhancing theory of mind in autism through humanoid robot interaction in a randomized controlled trial
sources.claim: In a registered randomized crossover trial, the iCub humanoid delivered ABA-based social-cognition role-play modules to children with autism in a clinical setting; the authors state explicitly that the robot was never autonomous in guiding ... and functioned as a tool under clinician supervision, and that children often needed real-time adjustments the robot could not make.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered structured instruction in cognition/social skills for children with autism, the closest analogue to the special-education strategies in this task. It shows state-of-the-art trials still require a human to guide and adapt the session.

sources.title: Can Milo the Robot Help Autistic Children Connect? | Edutopia
sources.claim: Milo, a humanoid robot sold to US school districts for autism instruction, runs pre-built social/emotional modules with a student, but the sessions are conducted with an educator present who works alongside the student; the robot delivers verbal prompts and facial cues rather than managing the instructional episode itself.
sources.transferJustification: Directly on task: a robot used in school special-education settings to teach communication and social-emotional skills. Cited to establish that deployed classroom robots operate as an adjunct with an educator, not as the instructor of record.

sources.title: Robot Guided 'Pen Skill' Training in Children with Motor Difficulties | PLOS One
sources.claim: A haptic robotic device (PHANTOM Omni stylus) delivered guided sensorimotor 'pen skill' training to 51 children aged 5-11 with manual control difficulties in a crossover study; children improved on the robot's own virtual task but showed no generalisation to standardised kinematic pen-skill assessments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered physical guidance for perceptual-motor skill training in children with motor difficulties, the closest analogue to hand-over-hand fine-motor instruction. Cited because it is the strongest such evidence and reports no transfer to real pen skills.

sources.title: QTrobot, our at home robot tutor for autism [Parent Testimonial]
sources.claim: In home use of QTrobot, the robot delivers pre-programmed 5-10 minute units while the child works on a tablet and an adult remains present as an assistant; the robot issues requests but the adult handles the rest of the interaction.
sources.transferJustification: Directly on task: robot-delivered early-years developmental instruction for a child with autism, including in an unstructured home setting. Cited to show that even the most teacher-like deployment requires a human assistant and is limited to tablet-mediated activities.

tasks.label: Encourage students to explore learning opportunities or persevere with challenging tasks to prepare them for later grades.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Whole-group circle time in a preschool special education classroom: the teacher uses enthusiastic praise, songs, visual supports and token boards to coax children with developmental delays into trying a new group activity (a new song, letter or counting game) and to keep attempting it when they lose interest.

One-on-one work on a challenging pre-academic or fine-motor task (puzzle, scissors, tracing a name) with a child who has a learning or physical disability: the teacher breaks the task into steps, uses a prompting hierarchy, and gives specific verbal encouragement so the child persists rather than quitting.

Free-choice/center time: the teacher encourages a child with autism or strong sensory preferences to leave a preferred routine and explore an unfamiliar center or material (sensory table, dramatic play, blocks), scaffolding curiosity and tolerating gradual approach over several sessions.

Encouragement delivered to a student who is nonverbal, deaf, or has a visual impairment, using sign language, tactile cues, an AAC device, or picture schedules to communicate 'keep going' and to invite exploration of new materials.

A frustration or refusal episode mid-task: the child cries, drops materials, or elopes; the teacher uses calming strategies, first-then boards, choice-giving and reinforcement to re-engage the child and get one more attempt at the challenging task.

tasks.label: Confer with parents, guardians, teachers, counselors, or administrators to resolve students' behavioral or academic problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Arrange indoor or outdoor space to facilitate creative play, motor-skill activities, or safety.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Before children arrive, the teacher arranges the indoor preschool special-education classroom for the day: positions child-sized tables and chairs, defines learning/play centers with low shelves, lays mats and cushions in the circle area, sets out toys and manipulatives at each center, and keeps floor pathways wide and clear for walkers and wheelchairs. Institution-run school/center classroom; no children present.

Mid-session, with 6-12 preschoolers with disabilities plus aides in the room: shifts furniture aside to open floor space for a movement song, removes scattered toys and tripping hazards from a child's mobility path, blocks off an unsafe area, and resets a center between activity rotations while children move unpredictably around the space.

Setting up specialized motor/sensory space indoors: assembling a gross-motor circuit from tunnels, foam wedges, balance beams, therapy balls and a mini-trampoline in the open area; positioning adaptive seating, standers and floor sitters; creating a quiet sensory corner with a tent, weighted items and dimmed lighting for a child who over-loads.

Outdoor play-yard setup on the school's fenced playground: wheeling out riding toys, balls, sand toys and cones, laying a mat or ramp over rough surfacing, arranging an adapted play area, and scanning the yard and equipment for hazards (debris, standing water, broken parts, loose mulch) and clearing them before children come out.

Periodic major reconfiguration (start of year, or when a child using a wheelchair enrolls): moving heavy shelving units, cubbies, storage bins and tables into a new floor plan, widening aisles, re-defining zones with dividers and rugs, and relocating equipment across the room.

Itinerant / home-based early-childhood special education visit: arranging a play space in a child's home or a community daycare room - clearing a floor area, moving household furniture aside, laying a mat, arranging toys within the child's reach, and removing small hazards before a motor-skill activity.

sources.developer: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
sources.title: ALORE: Autonomous Large-Object Rearrangement with a Legged Manipulator
sources.claim: ALORE, a legged mobile manipulator system, autonomously rearranges large objects (chairs, tables, bins) to target positions and orientations using onboard sensing, including 32 chairs over 40 minutes of continuous operation and a 40 m transport over uneven terrain and varying floor surfaces.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: moving furniture-scale objects (chairs, tables, bins) to specified target poses is the physical core of rearranging a classroom or play space; object sizes and placement precision are comparable, though demonstrated in an engineered lab/building setting.

sources.title: Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid passes 100,000-tote milestone in live GXO implementation
sources.claim: Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid is in commercial operation at a GXO warehouse, autonomously picking totes on and off mobile robots, loading conveyors and stacking containers at designated floor locations; over 100,000 totes moved.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: repeatedly transporting bulky containers from known presentation points to designated floor positions in an engineered workflow is the same physical operation as placing bins, mats and equipment at marked spots when the work is presented to the machine.

sources.title: RightHand Robotics Introduces the RightPick 4 System
sources.claim: RightHand Robotics' RightPick system performs autonomous piece-picking of diverse individual items in warehouse order-fulfilment cells, with tens of millions of items picked commercially.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: picking varied small items presented in totes and placing them into designated destinations matches setting out play materials at centers when items are presented fixtured in a purpose-built cell.

sources.title: Boston Dynamics' robot dog patrols 1.5 million-square-foot factory
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot runs autonomous inspection rounds inside a 1.5-million-sq-ft manufacturing facility, checking equipment and capturing 3D scans to flag anomalies.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: scheduled autonomous inspection rounds that detect anomalies on known assets transfer to the hazard-check portion of play-space preparation only where the route and asset set are fixed and machine-mapped.

sources.title: Figure humanoid robot cleans cluttered living room in new video demo
sources.claim: Figure demonstrated its Figure 03 humanoid, running the Helix 02 model, tidying a cluttered living-room set - picking up and sorting objects and wiping a surface - which the company states was done fully autonomously; it is a company demonstration, not a deployment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: putting scattered household objects away in a human-built room is the closest analogue to setting out and clearing play materials, but it is a curated single-room demo with no reliability data, so it does not establish worker-quality completion in a real facility.

sources.title: pi-0.5: a VLA with Open-World Generalization
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's pi-0.5 controls a mobile manipulator to clean ... homes never seen in training, but the developers state it does not always succeed and is far from perfect.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: tidying and putting objects in place in unseen rooms is the closest analogue to arranging a play space in a home or classroom; the developers' own statement of unreliability shows worker-quality completion is not established at E2/E3.

tasks.label: Serve meals or snacks in accordance with nutritional guidelines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Classroom snack time: in a self-contained preschool special-education room, the teacher portions the CACFP-compliant components (e.g., crackers/grain, cut fruit, milk) onto plates and cups at a small table, sets a serving in front of each of 6-12 children (some in adapted seating), checks allergy/texture restrictions against each child's plan, and refills seconds while supervising.

Cafeteria lunch service: the teacher walks the class to the school cafeteria, obtains or plates trays on the serving line, verifies each child's diet order (allergen-free, pureed/chopped, no-milk substitutions), carries trays to the table and places the correct one in front of each child, opens containers and cuts food.

Hands-on mealtime assistance: the teacher gives direct feeding support to one or two children with significant motor/oral-motor impairments — positioning the child, loading and guiding an adapted spoon hand-over-hand, pacing bites for aspiration safety, prompting self-feeding, and recording intake — while the rest of the group eats.

Family-style bulk portioning: a bulk hot/cold food delivery arrives from the central school kitchen in pans; the teacher measures required portion sizes into serving bowls and pitchers per the posted menu and nutrition standards, sets out child-size dishes, and stages the food for the meal.

Off-site or outdoor snack: on the playground, at a park during a field trip, or on a bus, the teacher distributes pre-packed snacks and drinks to each child, manages spills and allergy separation, and cleans up, with no fixed layout or equipment.

sources.title: Automating food production, one serving at a time - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Chef Robotics' autonomous meal-assembly pods use UR5e cobot arms with modular grippers to repeatedly dispense measured portions of rice, potatoes, sauces and cooked vegetables into meal trays moving down a production line at food manufacturers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: portioning and plating individual servings to a specified recipe/portion spec. It transfers to serving meals per nutritional guidelines because the objects (starches, cut vegetables, sauces), the required per-serving weight accuracy, and the deposit-into-a-dish motion are the same acts a teacher performs when portioning a compliant snack or meal.

sources.title: Chef Robotics, Packline Partner on End-to-End Meal Production Automation | Refrigerated & Frozen Foods
sources.claim: Chef Robotics' systems are in routine commercial production, with 83 million servings assembled at enterprise food manufacturers as of early 2026.

sources.system: Chef Robotics robots at Project Open Hand
sources.title: Project Open Hand | Chef Robotics case study
sources.claim: Two Chef robots work on Project Open Hand's conveyor line in San Francisco assembling medically tailored meals, a setting where precise per-serving portioning to nutrition specifications is the point of the work.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assembling medically tailored meal trays. It transfers because meeting a diet/nutrition prescription per portion is exactly the 'in accordance with nutritional guidelines' requirement, with comparable foods and portion tolerances.

sources.title: Sweetgreen accelerates deployment of automated kitchens | Restaurant Dive
sources.claim: Sweetgreen's Infinite Kitchen automated makeline moves bowls along a conveyor and dispenses portioned ingredients into them at up to 500 bowls per hour in operating restaurants, with more exact portions than manual assembly; humans still do prep and finishing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assembling an individual portioned serving to order for a specific diner. Transfers to plating a compliant meal/snack portion: same food types, same per-serving portion control, output handed off to the person who will eat it.

sources.title: Servi Q: The Compact Service Robot That Goes Where Others Can't — Bear Robotics
sources.claim: Bear Robotics' Servi is an ... mobile food-running and bussing robot deployed commercially in restaurants, senior living dining rooms and other hospitality venues; it transports loaded trays across the dining room but does not plate food or hand items to individual diners.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: food running in a dining room. Shows the ceiling of mobile food service in an institutional dining setting — transport of loaded trays — but not portioning, diet-order matching, or placing food in front of a specific child.

sources.system: School cafeteria cooking robots (Korea Institute for Robot Industry Advancement pilot)
sources.developer: Korea Institute for Robot Industry Advancement / Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education
sources.title: School hires robots as cafeteria chefs - The Korea Herald
sources.claim: Four fixed cooking robots (stir-fry, soup, deep-fry) operate in the canteen of Soonggok Middle School in Seoul to prepare lunches for about 660 students, with cafeteria staff still inspecting, washing and cutting ingredients and handling service.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: institutional school meal production. Relevant because it is the closest robotic deployment inside a school food operation; the robots are fixed stations loaded by staff and do not distribute food to students.

sources.title: Robotic system feeds people with severe mobility limitations | EurekAlert!
sources.claim: Cornell's EmPRISE lab demonstrated an autonomous robot-assisted feeding system that acquired bites and delivered them to the mouths of 13 people with severe mobility limitations across a lab, a medical center and one private home — a research evaluation, not a deployed product, and with cooperative adult users.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-assisted feeding of people who cannot self-feed. Directly comparable act, but demonstrated only with cooperative adults in a research study, without the pacing, positioning, prompting and aspiration-safety judgment a preschooler with disabilities requires.

sources.title: Kiri-Spoon: A Kirigami Utensil for Robot-Assisted Feeding (arXiv)
sources.claim: The Obi robotic feeder is a commercial four-bowl assistive dining device; it is not fully autonomous — the diner triggers each scoop and bite delivery with pressure switches, and a caregiver loads the bowls and teaches the delivery position.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assisted self-feeding. Shows the commercially available device for this act is user-triggered per bite and caregiver-set-up, so it does not substitute for a teacher providing mealtime assistance.

tasks.label: Organize and supervise games or other recreational activities to promote physical, mental, or social development.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Whole-class structured game in the special-education preschool classroom (parachute play, movement/song game, Simon Says, group ball game): teacher gathers 6-12 three-to-five-year-olds with mixed disabilities, sets out and adapts materials, gives visual/verbal/physical prompts, keeps non-participating children engaged, blocks unsafe behavior, ends and cleans up.

Outdoor playground or indoor gross-motor room session: teacher organizes an activity (obstacle course, chase game, riding toys, adapted equipment), positions herself for line-of-sight supervision, physically supports children with gait trainers/walkers or low tone, catches falls, mediates equipment-sharing, watches for elopement and mouthing hazards.

One-to-one or dyad adapted play game targeting IEP goals in a corner of the classroom or a therapy/play room: turn-taking board or ball game, cause-and-effect toy play, imitation/movement game with a child who may be nonverbal or motor-impaired; teacher runs the prompting hierarchy, keeps the child engaged for the session, and records data.

Free-play / learning-center rotation supervision: teacher circulates, scaffolds peer play among children with social-communication delays, redirects and resolves conflicts, keeps all children in view, manages toileting/sensory incidents, and transitions the group to the next activity.

Off-site or non-standard recreational activity: community park outing, inclusive playdate, family fun night, gym or pool visit; unfamiliar layout and equipment, other members of the public present, higher supervision demands and unpredictable conditions.

sources.title: Toddlers show increased physical activity with a robot playmate moving around the room | Oregon State University Newsroom
sources.claim: GoBot, a custom foam-padded wheeled assistive robot, autonomously ran movement-play sessions (keep-away routines, rewarding approach with lights/sounds/bubbles) with individual toddlers aged 2-3 in a dedicated playroom over two months, raising the children's physical activity; the autonomous routine engaged children as well as teleoperation.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family: running a play activity with a preschool-aged child to promote physical development. Objects (toys, padded robot, open playroom floor) and precision demands match a teacher-led gross-motor play session.

sources.developer: Oregon State University (Helmi, Fitter et al.)
sources.title: GoBot: An Autonomous Assistive Robot Using Behavior Trees to Encourage Child Mobility | ACM Transactions on Human-Robot Interaction
sources.claim: GoBot was given autonomous behavior-tree control for child-robot motion interventions, and the same group reported pilot observations of an autonomous red-light/green-light game robot interacting with children with disabilities.
sources.transferJustification: Directly relevant: an autonomous robot conducting a movement game (red light, green light) with young children including children with disabilities, i.e., a recreational activity organized to promote physical development.

sources.title: An Autonomous Robot-to-Group Exercise Coach at a Senior Living Community: A Study in Human-Robot Interaction
sources.claim: A NAO humanoid was programmed as an autonomous exercise instructor leading a warm-up and exercise routine for a group of residents at a senior living community.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: leading a group recreational/physical activity inside a human work facility. Transfer is limited, however: participants are cooperative, seated adults, and the robot neither supervises safety nor gives physical assistance.

sources.system: Pepper social robot in a school for autistic children
sources.developer: SoftBank Robotics platform; university research deployment
sources.title: "It's Important to Think of Pepper as a Teaching Aid or Resource External to the Classroom": A Social Robot in a School for Autistic Children
sources.claim: A Pepper robot placed in a school for autistic children was designed to run without wizard-of-Oz teleoperation, but its interactions were led by the children and it was framed as a teaching aid or resource external to the classroom rather than a substitute for the teacher.
sources.transferJustification: Same setting and population (school for children on the autism spectrum); shows current classroom social robots react to children rather than organizing and supervising an activity for a group.

sources.title: Living with Moxie, the robot companion for kids - Engadget
sources.claim: Moxie, a commercially sold companion robot, autonomously ran 15-25 minute play-based sessions of games, conversation and reading with an individual child at home (marketed for roughly ages 5-10).
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomously conducting play-based activities with a child to promote social-emotional development. Transfer is limited: one verbal, older child at a time, stationary robot, no materials handling and no safety supervision.

tasks.label: Organize and display students' work in a manner appropriate for their perceptual skills.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Classroom bulletin-board/wall display of 2-D work: teacher trims, backs and arranges a class set of paintings, scribble drawings and name-writing sheets by theme, mounts them at 3-4 year-old eye level on a cork board or wall with staples/pins/tape, and adds large simple name labels. Paper varies in size, is often wet-painted, curled, torn or has glued-on bits.

Organizing work into individual portfolios/folders/cubbies: collecting the week's mixed loose sheets from bins and tables, identifying whose work each piece is, dating it, filing into each child's folder/portfolio for IEP progress evidence, and putting take-home pieces into cubbies or backpacks.

Sensory-adapted display for children who are blind, low-vision or have other sensory needs: high-contrast backing, large-print and braille or tactile labels, textured/3-D pieces attached securely at reachable height so a child can explore by touch, with glare and clutter controlled.

Displaying 3-D work: fragile clay/playdough figures, block or recycled-material constructions, papier-mache and collage pieces arranged on a low shelf, table display or display case with name cards, without breaking them.

Hallway or school-entry display outside the classroom: seasonal change-out of backing paper, borders and cut letters on a large hall board, then mounting a class set of student work in an arranged grid, done while the corridor is in use.

sources.system: Fanuc M-710iC automated upholstery cell (integrator: Dvolu)
sources.title: Fanuc-powered robotic cell automates furniture upholstery process
sources.claim: A deployed, vision-guided Fanuc M-710iC work cell autonomously picks flexible fabric/cushion parts, positions, stretches, staples and trims them onto fixtured furniture components, adapting to part variation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic upholstery stapling. It is the same mechanical operation as mounting student work to a display board — handling limp sheet material, positioning it flat on a substrate presented in a fixture, and driving staples to hold it — at comparable precision, so performance transfers to a purpose-built display-mounting cell.

sources.system: Zünd cutting tables with Robotfactory cobots / PortaBase handling robots
sources.title: The Rise of Robotics: Automating Wide Format Print Production (FESPA)
sources.claim: Commercial cobot cells in wide-format print production autonomously place paper sheets and boards onto flatbeds in precise positions and pick and sort finished parts, at rates of a thousand boards per hour.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic sheet/board loading and part sorting in print finishing. It involves the same objects (single paper sheets and mounting boards) and the same precise flat placement required to lay out student work in a specified arrangement before fastening.

sources.title: Where Autonomy Works: Evaluating Robot Capabilities in 2026 (Epoch AI)
sources.claim: Amazon's Vulcan robotic arm is in production deployment picking items spanning a wide range of fragility and stowing them into compartments in a humanless robotic zone, calling for human help only in rare cases.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fragile mixed-item stowing into compartments. Placing varied delicate objects into a target compartment without damage is the same operation as setting fragile 3-D student pieces onto a display shelf; the source also notes such systems work only in zones designed around the robot.

sources.title: AmbiSort A-Series Named "Automated Picking Solution of the Year" by SupplyTech Breakthrough Awards
sources.claim: AmbiSort robotic picking systems autonomously pick mixed parcels and place them into destination containers at commercial scale, with over 100 million sorts across 80+ deployed robots.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic sortation of mixed items to labeled destinations. Filing each child's work into that child's folder is the same operation — read the destination marking, pick the item, place it in the right bin — at lower speed and comparable precision.

sources.system: USPS letter sorting machines with optical character readers
sources.title: Mail-Sorting Machines Are Crucial for the U.S. Postal Service (Scientific American)
sources.claim: Purpose-built postal sorting machines read handwritten as well as ... with optical character recognition and mechanically deposit each paper item into its destination, with humans reviewing only rare rejects.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated mail sorting. It establishes that a purpose-built machine can read handwritten names on paper and route each sheet to the correct individual destination bin, which is the identification-and-filing core of organizing children's work into per-child portfolios.

tasks.label: Plan and supervise experiential learning activities, such as class projects, field trips, or demonstrations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-group hands-on class project in the preschool special education classroom (art, sensory bin, cooking-adjacent craft): teacher plans the activity to IEP goals, sets out and adapts materials (adapted scissors, glue, paint, manipulatives), models the steps, gives hand-over-hand physical assistance, blocks mouthing/throwing, redirects behavior, and cleans up with the children.

Whole-class experiential demonstration at circle/table time (planting seeds, simple cooking, water/sink-float science, animal or sensory demo): teacher prepares equipment, physically demonstrates each step, passes materials to 8-12 children with mixed disabilities, manages hot/small/messy items and sensory reactions, and supports each child to take a turn.

On-campus experiential outing: school garden, playground exploration, or a walking 'field trip' to the cafeteria, library, or front office for life-skills practice; teacher plans the route and staffing, moves children with walkers/wheelchairs, watches for elopement, and prompts and physically assists each child through the target skill.

Off-site community field trip (zoo, farm, fire station, grocery store, city bus ride): teacher arranges permissions, transportation, adult-to-child ratios and medical/feeding needs, then supervises children in public spaces — holding hands, pushing strollers/wheelchairs, doing head counts, responding to meltdowns and toileting needs.

Visitor demonstration or special event brought into the classroom (firefighter in gear, therapy dog, dentist, musician, family cultural share): teacher plans and schedules it, pre-teaches with visuals, arranges seating and equipment, and supervises each child's turn interacting, providing physical support and calming children who are overwhelmed.

sources.title: LuxAI - Award winning social robots for autism and special needs education
sources.claim: QTrobot (LuxAI) is a commercially sold tabletop social robot deployed in special-needs schools, but it functions as a teacher-operated assistive tool that runs seated interaction modules; it does not handle materials, move around a classroom, or supervise children's activities.
sources.transferJustification: Closest deployed robot to preschool special education: it delivers social and communication learning modules to children with autism, bounding what classroom robots do today (seated verbal/visual prompting) and showing no capability to set up or supervise hands-on experiential activities.

sources.developer: LuxAI S.A. (deployment at Acorn Park School)
sources.title: Using Autism Robot to Engage Students with Autism
sources.claim: In specialist autism schools, QTrobot acts as a prompting 'third party' inside adult-led sessions, celebrating responses and giving verbal and visual prompts, while teaching staff run the activity.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (delivering adapted instruction to children with disabilities) shows the robot supplies prompts only, while the human educator plans, prepares materials, and supervises safety — the substance of this task.

sources.title: Encouraging classroom activities for children using avatar robots: a field trial
sources.claim: State-of-the-art robot participation in children's classroom activities is achieved by human teleoperators driving an avatar robot, not by autonomous control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (supporting and encouraging children during classroom activities) is the nearest analogue to supervising experiential learning; it required continuous remote human operation, so it cannot support an autonomous positive judgment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Control the inventory or distribution of classroom equipment, materials, or supplies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: During the instructional day, distributing materials to individual preschoolers with disabilities and to paraprofessionals: handing out crayons, adapted scissors, snack cups, manipulatives, communication cards and sensory items to the right child at a table or on the floor, refilling center bins mid-activity while 6-15 toddlers move around, mouth objects, and need hand-over-hand support.

End-of-activity and end-of-day collection, sorting and storage of classroom materials: gathering toys, blocks, puzzle pieces and art supplies off tables, floor and cubbies, sanitizing them, and returning each to its labeled bin, shelf or locked cabinet in the classroom.

Periodic inventory control: walking the classroom cabinets and closet, counting consumables (paper, glue, gloves, wipes, diapers, laminating film), checking assistive-technology and adaptive equipment against an equipment log, and filling out/submitting requisitions or supply orders to the school office.

Retrieving and transporting supplies between the school's central stockroom/office/copy room and the classroom: loading a cart or boxes of paper, curriculum kits and consumables, moving them through school corridors and elevators, and delivering them into the classroom or to a colleague's room.

Start/end-of-year setup and teardown: unpacking new deliveries, labeling and re-organizing storage, and assembling individualized student kits and adapted materials (laminating, cutting picture cards, attaching Velcro, building visual schedules and sensory boxes) for each child's IEP.

sources.title: How Diligent's Robots Are Making a Difference in Texas Hospitals - IEEE Spectrum
sources.claim: Moxi, a mobile manipulator, autonomously picks supplies out of hospital supply closets and delivers them to patient rooms in working hospitals.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fetching and delivering consumable supplies from a central store to a work room inside an institutional building. Comparable objects (boxed/bagged consumables), comparable precision (grasp, transport, hand-off) and the same class of environment (institutional corridors with people present), so it carries over to a school stockroom-to-classroom supply run.

sources.title: Swisslog Healthcare Partners with Diligent Robotics to Enhance Hospital Logistics – Ortho Spine News
sources.claim: Moxi is a commercial product deployed at scale, with more than 25 US hospitals and over one million completed deliveries.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes deployed maturity and reliability of the supply-transport capability cited for the stockroom-to-classroom instance.

sources.title: AmbiSort A-Series Named "Automated Picking Solution of the Year" by SupplyTech Breakthrough Awards
sources.claim: AmbiSort robotic cells autonomously pick and place mixed, varied items presented in bulk and sort them into designated output locations in commercial logistics operations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sorting heterogeneous items presented to a fixtured cell into labeled destination containers. That is the E1 form of putting classroom materials away into labeled bins - similar object diversity and grasp precision, with the work presented to the machine.

sources.title: Ambi Robotics: AmbiSort A-Series Full-Stack Solution - Material Handling 24/7
sources.claim: AmbiSort cells run in production at high throughput and above 99% sorting accuracy with one associate overseeing several robots.
sources.transferJustification: Substantiates worker-quality reliability and limited human intervention for the fixtured sorting/put-away capability transferred to classroom material storage at E1.

sources.title: Amazon introduces Sparrow—a state-of-the-art robot that handles millions of diverse products
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm detects, selects and handles individual products drawn from a highly diverse inventory inside fenced fulfillment-center cells.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: singulating and transferring small, varied consumer goods (the same size and weight class as classroom consumables and manipulatives) between totes in a purpose-built cell, supporting the E1 form of sorting and storing supplies.

sources.title: SpartanNash deploys Simbe Tally robots in 60 more grocery stores - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Tally is an autonomous shelf-scanning inventory robot deployed across grocery chains; the data it collects drives stocking and ordering decisions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: auditing stock on shelving and feeding replenishment ordering - the same count-and-reorder loop as a classroom supply inventory, performed on machine-readable, planogrammed shelving (the E1 presentation of the stock).

sources.title: Telexistence to install AI re-stocking robots in 300 convenience stores across Japan
sources.claim: TX SCARA restocking robots autonomously replenish beverage shelves in hundreds of convenience stores, with remote operators intervening only in rare error cases.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: replenishing standardized stock into fixed, machine-known shelf positions with only occasional remote assistance; supports the E1 restocking/put-away form where storage locations are fixtured and known to the machine.

roles.description: Teach academic, social, and life skills to kindergarten students with learning, emotional, or physical disabilities. Includes teachers who specialize and work with students who are blind or have visual impairments; students who are deaf or have hearing impairments; and students with intellectual disabilities.

tasks.label: Instruct students with disabilities in academic subjects, using a variety of techniques, such as phonetics, multisensory learning, or repetition to reinforce learning and meet students' varying needs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-group phonics/phonemic awareness lesson in a kindergarten resource room or inclusive classroom: teacher models letter-sound correspondences with sound cards and letter tiles, elicits choral and individual responses, corrects errors, and uses repetition and cumulative review across 4-6 children with mixed disabilities.

One-on-one multisensory literacy instruction (Orton-Gillingham style) with a student with a specific learning disability: teacher says the sound, has the child trace letters in sand or on textured cards, sometimes guiding the child's hand, and repeats drills until the child responds accurately.

Early numeracy instruction for students with intellectual/developmental disabilities using manipulatives (counting bears, ten frames, number lines), massed and distributed trials, prompting hierarchies, and immediate reinforcement, with data collected on each trial.

Instruction adapted for sensory disability: teaching pre-braille/braille letters and tactile graphics to a student who is blind, or delivering the same academic content in ASL with visual supports to a deaf student, adjusting pace and modality to the child's responses.

Co-taught whole-class academic lesson in a general education kindergarten, where the special educator differentiates content on the fly, re-teaches to individual students, redirects behavior of students with emotional/behavioral disabilities, and reinforces target skills through repetition.

instances.label: Self-contained or resource-room 1:1 / small-group language and communication instruction with kindergartners with autism or intellectual disability: teacher runs discrete-trial or naturalistic language trials, presents picture cards, models an AAC device or PECS exchange, uses a prompting hierarchy (gestural through full physical hand-over-hand prompts), delivers immediate reinforcement, and records trial-by-trial data while managing attention and behavior.

Fine-motor / perceptual-motor instruction: pre-writing strokes, tracing, scissors, pegboards, lacing, beads, playdough, adaptive pencil grips and slant boards. Teacher positions the materials and the child, physically shapes the grasp, gives hand-over-hand or hand-under-hand guidance, and fades support across repetitions.

Gross-motor and sensory-integration activity: movement circuits, balance beam, ball and bilateral-coordination games, sensory bins, weighted or deep-pressure input, sensory-room or gym routines; includes physically supporting, spotting, or repositioning a child with motor impairment and adjusting the activity when a child becomes dysregulated.

Multisensory cognition/memory instruction in an inclusive kindergarten class: counting bears, ten-frames, letter tiles, sorting trays, matching/memory games, visual schedules and mnemonic routines. The teacher circulates among several children, re-presents materials, adapts the strategy on the fly, and cues recall.

Sensory-disability-specific instruction: tactile/pre-braille literacy with braille cards, tactile graphics and a braille writer for a blind kindergartner (hand-under-hand exploration), or signed/auditory-training instruction, listening checks and hearing-aid/FM device troubleshooting for a deaf or hard-of-hearing kindergartner, plus basic orientation and mobility practice in the hallway.

Incidental/embedded teaching during play centers, snack, and transitions: modeling and prompting turn-taking in the block or dramatic-play corner, expanding utterances, prompting imitation, physically redirecting or blocking unsafe behavior, and guiding a dysregulated child through a calming routine before resuming the target skill.

sources.title: Social robots for education: a global analysis of deployments in real scenarios
sources.claim: Milo (RoboKind) humanoid robots are commercially deployed in North American schools to deliver social-skills and academic lessons to autistic students, as a curriculum-delivery tool within the Robots4Autism program rather than as a substitute for the teacher.
sources.transferJustification: Closest deployed analogue to the rated task: robot-delivered special-education lessons for young students with disabilities in school classrooms.

sources.system: Milo (RoboKind) classroom implementation, Marshall County schools
sources.title: Implementation Insights: "Breakfast Buddies" with Marshall County
sources.claim: In actual school implementations a human facilitator sits with a tablet and runs each Milo lesson, selecting and advancing content and managing the students; the robot does not conduct the session on its own.
sources.transferJustification: Direct evidence on how robot-mediated special-education instruction is actually operated: a human educator runs the lesson, so the robot does not complete the instructional task with limited intervention.

sources.system: Milo / Robots4Autism (Spartanburg School District case study)
sources.title: IESD Case Study: Children on the Autism Spectrum Show Improvement with Robots4Autism
sources.claim: Earlier school deployments of Milo followed the same pattern: an autism specialist acted as facilitator for pull-out one-on-one sessions and controlled the lesson from a separate iPad.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family (special-education instruction of young students with disabilities); shows the human specialist, not the robot, employs and adapts the instructional strategy.

sources.title: UNESCO Report Highlights Schools' Successful Use of QTrobot for Inclusive Education
sources.claim: QTrobot is used in special-needs schools as a structured-lesson tool operated by teachers and teaching assistants, i.e., an aid inside the adult-run lesson rather than an autonomous instructor.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family (special-education instruction for children with autism/SEN in schools); establishes that the state-of-the-art commercial classroom robot is teacher-operated.

sources.title: Second Language Tutoring using Social Robots. A Large-Scale Study.
sources.claim: A large-scale preregistered study had an autonomous social robot tutor deliver seven one-on-one vocabulary lessons to five-year-olds in schools; gains merely matched a tablet application, and the interaction was a narrow screen-paired word drill with no physical handling or behavior management.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (autonomous robot tutoring of kindergarten-aged children in schools); marks the ceiling of autonomous robot instruction — a single scripted verbal/screen drill with typically developing children, far short of special-education strategy use with physical prompting.

sources.system: Social robots in education (Milo, Kaspar, NAO, QTrobot) — review of real deployments
sources.developer: multiple (RoboKind, University of Hertfordshire, SoftBank Robotics, LuxAI)
sources.title: Social robots for education: a global analysis of deployments in real scenarios
sources.claim: Reviews of real classroom social-robot deployments conclude these robots are conceived as supplements that add value alongside human teachers, not as systems that carry out teaching themselves.
sources.transferJustification: Synthesis of the deployment literature for exactly this task family (robot-supported instruction, including special education), establishing that no fielded system performs the teacher's instructional role end to end.
