tasks.label: Instruct and monitor students in the use and care of equipment or materials to prevent injuries and damage.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start-of-activity instruction to a small group or whole resource-room class: teacher demonstrates safe handling of ordinary classroom materials (scissors, glue, pencils, manipulatives, iPads/Chromebooks), states rules for putting them away, then circulates among 4-12 elementary students with mixed disabilities, correcting grips, redirecting misuse, and physically taking back a tool that is being waved or thrown.

One-on-one hands-on teaching for a student with significant intellectual or motor disability: hand-over-hand or partial physical prompting to use adapted equipment (loop scissors, adapted utensils, switch toys, an AAC speech device), fading prompts across trials, positioning the student and device, and preventing the student from mouthing, dropping, or slamming the equipment.

Sensory-disability equipment instruction and care: teaching a student who is blind to hold, fold, and store a white cane or load and clean a braille writer/notetaker, or teaching a deaf/hard-of-hearing student to insert, check the battery on, and store hearing aids and an FM/DM receiver; includes daily equipment checks and reteaching after misuse.

Life-skills or activity-setting instruction in a school kitchen, gym, or playground: teaching and supervising safe use of a toaster, microwave, knives, cleaning supplies, PE apparatus, or playground equipment for students with impulsivity, poor motor planning, or seizure risk; teacher stays within arm's reach and blocks unsafe actions.

Reactive monitoring during dysregulation or transitions: a student begins chewing a cord, banging a tablet, throwing chairs or materials, or grabbing another student's equipment; teacher moves in, verbally cues, physically secures or removes the item, and reteaches the expectation, documenting the incident.

sources.title: Range Helps Bring Special Education Robot to Classrooms
sources.claim: The RoboKind Milo humanoid is deployed in elementary special education programs, but it delivers scripted verbal/social-emotional lesson modules alongside a human teacher or therapist; it does not manipulate classroom tools, teach equipment handling, or physically intervene with students.
sources.transferJustification: Closest related task: robot-delivered instruction to elementary students with disabilities in a school (E2). Cited to show the state of the art is speech-based lesson delivery with a human facilitator, with no handling of materials or safety intervention, so it does not transfer to instructing and monitoring equipment use.

sources.system: SoftBank Pepper (school wellbeing deployment, Lemaignan et al. 2022)
sources.title: CARE: towards customized assistive robot-based education (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: A SoftBank Pepper humanoid ran autonomously in a school corridor interacting with students diagnosed with autism, showing autonomous social operation in a school setting but no object handling, equipment instruction, or safety supervision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous social interaction with students inside a school (E2 setting). It substantiates only conversational presence; the cited work involves no manipulation of tools, no monitoring for unsafe equipment use, and no physical intervention, so capability does not carry over.

sources.title: Encouraging classroom activities for children using avatar robots: a field trial (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: Field trials that put robots into routine elementary classroom activities rely on human remote operators rather than autonomy, indicating that classroom-level supervision and interaction with children is still teleoperated.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot participation in whole-classroom activities with elementary students. It is continuously teleoperated, so under the autonomy rule it cannot support a positive judgment for instructing or monitoring students.

tasks.label: Prepare, administer, or grade tests or assignments to evaluate students' progress.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Organize and display students' work in a manner appropriate for their perceptual skills.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Weekly refresh of the classroom bulletin board/wall display: teacher selects recent work from 8–12 students with mixed disabilities, trims and backs pieces on construction paper, hand-letters or prints large-high-contrast titles and name labels, and staples/pins the pieces onto a corkboard in an uncluttered layout hung low enough for students to see and touch. Done in an occupied or just-vacated elementary special-ed classroom, on a ladder or step stool, working around furniture, sensory equipment and existing decor.

Preparing a display outside the classroom: mounting student work in a hallway board, locked display case, or school art-show table for parent night. Requires trimming/mounting, adding captions in print and braille, hanging at child eye level in a corridor with foot traffic, and matting or framing a few pieces.

Organizing accumulated work: collecting the day's/week's completed papers from desks and bins, dating and labeling them, sorting them by student into individual folders, portfolios, binders or cubbies (picture-symbol, color-coded, or brailled tabs), keeping IEP-evidence samples in order and sending the rest home in take-home folders.

Building an adapted display for a student who is blind or has low vision or significant motor/perceptual impairments: mounting raised-line drawings, textured collage, and puffy-paint work on a tactile board or slant board within reach, adding braille and large-print labels, spacing items widely on a plain high-contrast background, and securing pieces so they survive tactile exploration.

Individual, desk-level presentation of work: taping a finished paper to a student's desk or work surface, setting work on an adapted easel/slant board or in a personal magnetic display frame, arranging three-dimensional projects (clay, block constructions, craft objects) on a table or shelf for an IEP meeting or classroom visit, and repositioning items for each child's visual field and reach.

sources.title: Gemini Robotics 1.5
sources.claim: Frontier generalist manipulation models perform fine paper/object manipulation (e.g., origami folding, packing) in fixed laboratory workcells, but nothing in the released capability set covers assembling or mounting a display of student work.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: dexterous manipulation of thin/deformable items on a lab table. It shows the frontier of autonomous paper handling, but demonstrations are single tabletop manipulations, not assembling a captioned, arranged wall display, so it does not substantiate completion of the display instances.

sources.developer: United States Postal Service / Siemens-ElectroCom, Lockheed Martin
sources.title: Real-time operating system sorts mail fast
sources.claim: Purpose-built automated sorters read each paper item and drive it into a designated destination bin, sorting tens of thousands of flat paper pieces per hour with no human handling between feed and bin.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sorting individual sheets of paper into per-recipient destination bins in sequence. Objects (loose flat paper), the required precision (correct bin, correct order) and the purpose-built feeder/bin environment match filing student worksheets into per-student folders when the work is presented to the machine.

sources.title: Inside a USPS Sorting Center: How Your Mail Gets Sorted
sources.claim: Automated mail-processing equipment in current use reads each piece and directs it into the correct bin, including sequencing passes that order items by destination.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as the DBCS item: machine-controlled distribution of paper documents into labeled destination pockets, which is the physical core of filing student work into individual student folders in a purpose-built cell.

sources.title: Figure AI says its humanoid robots ran 24 hours straight sorting packages
sources.claim: Humanoid robots ran a multi-hour autonomous package-sorting shift in a warehouse, showing autonomous item-to-destination sorting outside a fixed feeder machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous sorting of discrete items into destinations at a fixed station fed by a conveyor. Supports machine-controlled sorting when the work is presented, but the objects are rigid parcels, not loose children's papers, and the station is engineered around the robot.

sources.title: corobos: A Design for Mobile Robots Enabling Cooperative Transitions between Table and Wall Surfaces
sources.claim: The closest research demonstration of robotic wall display involves centimetre-scale swarm robots repositioning a ~1 gram poster on an instrumented wall, with a person attaching the poster to the robot and one robot commanding the other.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: positioning a paper item on a wall. It falls short of this task because a human attaches the poster, the item weighs about a gram, the wall is instrumented for the robots, and no trimming, fastening or captioning is performed.

sources.system: High-speed robot hand single-sheet separation system
sources.title: Single-Sheet Separation from Paper Stack Based on Friction Uncertainty Using High-Speed Robot Hand
sources.claim: Laboratory work has demonstrated a high-speed robotic hand separating a single sheet from a paper stack, indicating that even basic single-sheet handling by general robot hands is still a research problem.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: picking one sheet of paper from a stack, a prerequisite for mounting or filing student work. It substantiates only the pick step in a laboratory rig, not the whole instance.

sources.developer: Realbotix / Salamanca City Central School District
sources.title: Salamanca, N.Y., Schools to Pilot AI Robot Teaching Assistant
sources.claim: Robots actually being placed in US elementary/secondary classrooms are stationary conversational tutors without manipulators; no deployed school robot organizes or mounts student work.
sources.transferJustification: Context for negative judgments: the only robots deployed in classrooms as of 2026 provide verbal tutoring and do not physically handle classroom materials.

tasks.label: Organize and supervise games or other recreational activities to promote physical, mental, or social development.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Adapted PE / gross-motor game block in the school gym or multipurpose room: teacher sets out cones, balls, parachute, bean bags; leads a modified game (bowling, target toss, relay, parachute) for 4-8 elementary students with mixed disabilities; demonstrates, gives hand-over-hand or physical prompts, keeps students in bounds, stops unsafe behavior, packs equipment away.

Structured recess / outdoor play period on the school playground: teacher escorts a group out, organizes a structured game (tag variant, four square, buddy game), prompts peer interaction for a student with autism or intellectual disability, scans for safety, breaks up conflicts, responds to falls or elopement, lines students up to return.

Small-group indoor social-skills or cooperative game in the classroom or resource room: 3-6 students play a board game, card game, or turn-taking activity with physical materials; teacher sets rules, cues turn-taking and sharing, redirects off-task or escalating behavior, adapts rules for a nonverbal or physically limited student, cleans up.

Sensory/motor circuit or play activity in a self-contained classroom or motor room for students with significant support needs: obstacle course, ball pit, swing, therapy-ball activity; teacher physically supports, positions, and sometimes transfers students, manages equipment, watches for seizures/self-injury, and follows OT/PT plans.

One-on-one recreational/social game session with a single student at a table (emotion-matching game, perspective-taking or turn-taking game, simple board or tablet game) targeting an IEP social goal, in a quiet classroom corner or therapy room with a compliant, seated student.

Off-campus or special-event recreation: community outing (bowling alley, park, pool), Special Olympics practice, or field day; teacher organizes the activity in a setting not controlled by the school, supervises students amid crowds, traffic, and unfamiliar equipment.

sources.system: Jibo in-home socially assistive robot system (Yale Social Robotics Lab)
sources.developer: Yale University (Scassellati et al.) / Jibo Inc.
sources.title: Improving social skills in children with ASD using a long-term, in-home social robot | Science Robotics
sources.claim: An autonomous tabletop social robot (Jibo) conducted daily one-on-one social-skills game activities (emotional storytelling, perspective-taking, sequencing) with 12 children with ASD aged 6-12 for 30 days, producing measured gains in social communication.
sources.transferJustification: Directly on point for the one-on-one variant of the task: the robot organizes and runs game activities whose stated purpose is social development, with children of the same age and disability profile served by elementary special education teachers.

sources.system: Jibo in-home socially assistive robot system
sources.title: Improving social skills in children with ASD using a long-term, in-home social robot | Science Robotics
sources.claim: The same in-home robot intervention required a caregiver to participate with the child in every 30-minute session, i.e. an adult was part of the interaction rather than the robot working with the child alone.
sources.transferJustification: Same system as evidence 0; documents the degree of human involvement, which bears on whether the robot can carry a session without an adult present.

sources.system: Pepper autonomous exercise facilitator (ASBLab, University of Toronto)
sources.developer: University of Toronto Autonomous Systems and Biomechatronics Lab (SoftBank Pepper hardware)
sources.title: Long-Term Exercise Assistance: Group and One-on-One Interactions between a Social Robot and Seniors (Robotics 12(1):9)
sources.claim: A Pepper robot autonomously facilitated nine upper-body exercises in both group and one-on-one sessions with older adults in a long-term care facility, adapting to user affect and monitoring heart rate over a long-term study.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: organizing and leading a group physical-activity session to promote physical wellbeing inside an institutional facility. Transfer to this task is limited: participants are seated, cooperative adults, the robot handles no equipment, gives no physical assistance, and performs no safety supervision of mobile children.

sources.developer: Oregon State University (Naomi Fitter, Colleges of Engineering and Health)
sources.title: Toddlers show increased physical activity with a robot playmate moving around the room | OSU Newsroom
sources.claim: A custom mobile robot playmate (GoBot) ran an autonomous keep-away play routine that raised toddlers' physical activity in a playroom, one child at a time, with researchers present; developers state it is not intended to replace caregivers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: eliciting physical activity through play with young children. Transfer is partial: the robot elicits movement but does not organize a game with rules, manage a group, or supervise safety.

sources.title: Robokind's Milo Robot: Communication and Social Skills Practice for Learners with Autism
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo robot is commercially deployed in US school districts for autism social-skills instruction, used in weekly or biweekly one-to-one sessions run with a teacher/facilitator, not as an unsupervised activity leader.
sources.transferJustification: Closest commercially deployed school system for social-skills activities; shows the deployed pattern is a facilitator-run one-to-one lesson, not robot supervision of a group recreational activity.

sources.title: QTrobot for special needs education - LuxAI S.A.
sources.claim: QTrobot, marketed for special-needs education with curricula of educational units, is designed to be operated ... teacher, parent or therapist, indicating operator-selected content rather than autonomous session management.
sources.transferJustification: Widely marketed special-education robot; documents that classroom use is adult-operated, so it cannot substantiate autonomous organization and supervision of an activity.

sources.system: Socially assistive robotics field survey (Escaping Oz)
sources.title: Escaping Oz: Autonomy in Socially Assistive Robotics | Annual Reviews
sources.claim: A review of socially assistive robotics notes the field routinely relies on Wizard-of-Oz control or teleoperation to overcome technical limits, so most reported child-robot therapy/education interactions are not autonomous.
sources.transferJustification: Background on the autonomy status of the child-robot interaction literature relied on for this task; supports treating unclear demonstrations as teleoperated.

tasks.label: Administer standardized ability and achievement tests to elementary students with special needs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Plan or supervise experiential learning activities, such as class projects, field trips, demonstrations, or visits by guest speakers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Self-contained or resource classroom hands-on class project (science experiment, art/build project) with 6-12 elementary students with mixed learning, emotional, or physical disabilities plus a paraprofessional: teacher plans the activity, gathers and preps materials, sets up stations, models the steps, then circulates supervising — giving physical/hand-over-hand prompting, managing scissors/glue/tools safety, redirecting behavior, and running cleanup.

In-school life-skills demonstration and supervised practice (cooking in the life-skills kitchen, laundry, hygiene, money handling) for students with intellectual disabilities: teacher plans and sequences the task, demonstrates each step, then supervises students using appliances, hot surfaces, or knives, providing hands-on assistance and continuous safety monitoring.

Off-campus community-based instruction / field trip (grocery store, zoo, museum, public bus ride): teacher plans logistics, permissions and staffing, then escorts and supervises the group in public — managing wheelchairs and mobility, keeping every student in sight in crowds, handling sensory overload or elopement, restrooms, and transitions on and off the bus.

Guest speaker visit, school assembly, or in-school demonstration (firefighter, therapy dog, science show): teacher coordinates scheduling and logistics with the visitor, preps the room and AV, prepares students in advance, then seats and supports students during the event — prompting, interpreting/simplifying content, and managing behavior and sensory needs.

Experiential activity in shared school spaces (school garden planting, nature/measurement walk on school grounds, library or gym project): teacher plans the activity, transports tools and materials, then supervises students working in a semi-open school area with other classes and staff present.

sources.title: Realbotix to Deploy First Humanoid Robot and AI Teachers Assistant in U.S. School District
sources.claim: Realbotix's Optio AI teacher's assistant with an M-Series humanoid is being piloted in a US school district, but functions as a conversational tutoring avatar/robot for concept reinforcement and homework help; it is described as not mobile and does not set up materials, run hands-on projects, or supervise students.
sources.transferJustification: Closest available system in the task's own setting (a school). Cited to show the frontier of classroom robots is verbal tutoring, not planning/supervising experiential activities, which require material handling and student safety supervision.

sources.system: Realbotix humanoid 'Sally' at Salamanca City Central School District
sources.developer: Realbotix Corp. / Salamanca City Central School District
sources.title: Salamanca, N.Y., Schools to Pilot AI Robot Teaching Assistant
sources.claim: Coverage of the same pilot confirms the classroom humanoid is limited to curriculum-programmed tutoring and reinforcement and is not mobile, so it cannot escort students, handle materials, or supervise an activity.
sources.transferJustification: Same school setting as the task; establishes the functional ceiling (verbal tutoring, immobile) of deployed classroom robots relative to supervising hands-on activities.

sources.title: Frontiers | CARE: towards customized assistive robot-based education
sources.claim: A Pepper humanoid was left to operate autonomously ... a school corridor, engaging students in social interaction; the deployment involved conversational interaction only, with no supervision of activities, material handling, or physical assistance to students.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (autonomous social interaction with students in a school). Shows autonomous school robots achieve dialogue and presence, not the object handling, safety monitoring, and physical prompting that supervising experiential activities requires.

sources.system: Pepper / Kaspar in special educational needs schools
sources.title: Social Robots: A Promising Tool to Support People with Autism. A Systematic Review of Recent Research and Critical Analysis from the Clinical Perspective
sources.claim: Reviews of social robots in special education report deployments such as Pepper in a special educational ..., used for structured interaction sessions rather than for organizing or supervising class projects, trips, or demonstrations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (robot-mediated sessions with the same student population). Establishes that special-education robot use is interaction support under adult supervision, not autonomous planning or supervision of experiential learning activities.

Includes teachers who specialize and work with students who are blind or have visual impairments; students who are deaf or have hearing impairments; and students with intellectual disabilities.

instances.label: Duplicating and assembling print materials for the day's lessons: walking to the school workroom, running off modified/leveled worksheets and reading packets on the copier, collating, stapling, trimming, and carrying sorted stacks back to the resource room.

Arranging the classroom space before an activity: pushing desks/tables into small-group pods or station clusters, moving chairs, clearing floor space and widening aisles for a wheelchair or walker, positioning a kidney table for small-group instruction.

Laying out hands-on activity materials at stations: filling task boxes and per-student trays with math manipulatives, counters, sorting cards, science kit parts, scissors/glue/paper, and setting one set at each student's desk or station.

Producing adapted/accessible materials: embossing braille or printing large-print versions, making tactile graphics, laminating picture cards, visual schedules and token boards, then cutting them out and attaching Velcro.

Setting up equipment and assistive technology: pulling out and powering student laptops/tablets, logging in and loading the lesson app, connecting an AAC device or switch, turning on and aiming the projector/interactive board, positioning adaptive seating or a stander.
Resetting and cleaning the room between classes: wiping tables, sanitizing shared manipulatives and sensory items, putting materials back into labeled bins and restocking supply caddies.

sources.title: Amazon robotics: Meet the robots inside fulfillment centers
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm autonomously identifies and picks individual, varied items out of containers and places them into specific totes in fulfillment centers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: order-item picking into totes. Transfers to laying out per-student material sets: same class of small, mixed, loosely-presented objects (cards, counters, small tools) picked and placed into a designated receptacle at comparable precision, inside a fenced cell.

sources.title: Amazon robotics: Meet the robots inside fulfillment centers
sources.claim: Amazon's Proteus is a fully autonomous mobile robot that lifts and moves wheeled carts to designated locations while navigating a facility with people present.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: repositioning wheeled carts (GoCarts) to specified spots. Transfers to arranging wheeled classroom furniture into a target layout when the furniture is on robot-liftable bases and target positions are marked, as in a purpose-built setting.

sources.system: Danfoss/VARO kitting cell with Roboception rc_viscore 3D vision
sources.title: Case Studies: Automated Kitting Solution with 3D Robot Vision
sources.claim: A production kitting cell at Danfoss uses a robot with 3D vision to pick an assortment of different parts from pallets and assemble them into trays, adapting autonomously to changes in part presentation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: industrial kitting. Transfers to assembling per-student material trays and restocking labeled bins: mixed small items gathered from bulk containers into a defined tray set, with the robot adapting to shifted part positions.

sources.system: Xerox Production Ready Booklet Maker Finisher (Versant press family); Plockmatic PowerSquare inline folder/stapler
sources.title: Production Ready (PR) Booklet Maker Finisher – Xerox technical documentation
sources.claim: Production print finishers automatically collate, staple/saddle-stitch, fold and trim printed sheets inline, producing finished sets without a human handling each sheet.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: duplicating and finishing document sets. Same physical output as a teacher's collated, stapled worksheet packets; the machine handles feeding, collating, stapling and trimming when jobs are presented to it as in a print shop.

sources.title: Braille Printers | American Foundation for the Blind
sources.claim: Commercial braille embossers automatically produce braille text and high-resolution tactile graphics, including automatic double-sided embossing, directly from a computer file.
sources.transferJustification: Directly covers the embossing/tactile-graphic production step of preparing adapted materials for students who are blind: paper is loaded and the machine produces the finished accessible page unattended.

sources.system: HCP-A100 Automatic Plastic Card Lamination System
sources.title: Automatic Plastic Card Lamination System (HCP-A100)
sources.claim: Fully automatic card lamination and cut-to-registration lines laminate and cut sheet stock into finished cards at production rates without per-item human handling.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: laminating and die-cutting card stock. Same physical operation as laminating and cutting picture cards, visual schedules and token boards, performed on machine-fed sheets in a purpose-built line.

sources.title: Alphabet's X has 'Everyday Robots' test fleet that autonomously performs office maintenance tasks
sources.claim: Alphabet's Everyday Robots operated a fleet of over 100 mobile manipulators autonomously performing office chores, including wiping cafeteria tables with a squeegee attachment, on Google campuses.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: wiping tables in a shared human facility. Covers the surface-wiping element of resetting a classroom, though only as a prototype fleet and not the sanitizing/restocking elements.

sources.title: Avidbots releases floor-scrubbing robot for industrial spaces – The Robot Report
sources.claim: Avidbots' Neo autonomous floor scrubber ... commercially deployed cleaning floors in human facilities including schools, airports and warehouses.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous floor cleaning inside school buildings. Shows navigation of an occupied school facility (E2) for a cleaning task, but covers only open floor area, not table wiping, sanitizing manipulatives or restocking bins.

tasks.label: Instruct students in daily living skills required for independent maintenance and self-sufficiency, such as hygiene, safety, and food preparation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Life-skills classroom kitchen in a middle school: teacher leads a small group (3-8 students with intellectual/developmental disabilities) through a cooking routine (handwashing, measuring, spreading, microwave/toaster-oven use, cleanup) using task analysis and least-to-most prompting, including modeling and hand-over-hand guidance, while physically preventing burns/cuts and taking data on each student's steps.

Personal hygiene and grooming instruction in the classroom or school restroom: toothbrushing, handwashing, deodorant, hair care, menstrual care, dressing. Teacher demonstrates on self/models, physically prompts and repositions students (some with motor impairments), manages privacy and dignity, and fades prompts across sessions.

Classroom safety instruction with props and role play: fire/lockdown drill practice, appliance and kitchen safety, reading warning labels, stranger/internet safety, simulated pedestrian crossing. Largely verbal and visual instruction plus supervised hands-on practice, with behavior redirection of adolescents.

Community-based instruction: teacher escorts 2-4 students to a grocery store, fast-food counter, or public bus stop to practice shopping, ordering, paying, and street crossing; models and prompts in situ, handles crowds, traffic, strangers, and student elopement risk.

Instruction adapted for sensory impairments: teaching a student who is blind tactile/hand-under-hand techniques for safe knife, stove, and grooming tasks and tactile labeling; or teaching a deaf student the same daily living routines in ASL with visual demonstration, in a resource room or life-skills room.

sources.system: Kebbi socially assistive robot instruction study
sources.title: Socially Assistive Robotic Instruction for Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder
sources.claim: Socially assistive robots used for instruction of children with autism are small tabletop platforms without manipulation ability, run alongside a tablet and a computer operated by a human instructor, i.e. the robot delivers scripted prompts while a person runs the session.
sources.transferJustification: Closest related task: robot-delivered instruction to students with disabilities. It shows the state of the art is a screen-faced tabletop robot with no ability to demonstrate cooking or hygiene, physically prompt, or supervise safety, so capability does not transfer to daily-living-skills instruction.

sources.system: Kiwi and other SAR platforms for autism support
sources.title: A Review of Socially Assistive Robotics in Supporting Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
sources.claim: Reviews of socially assistive robots for children with autism report that these classroom robots are operated through Wizard-of-Oz interfaces by a human, rather than running instructional sessions autonomously.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-assisted teaching/therapy sessions with children with disabilities. Human control of the robot's moves disqualifies it as autonomous completion of an instructional session, so it cannot substantiate teaching daily living skills.

sources.title: Can a robot open new doors to teach social interaction to children with autism?
sources.claim: Educational robot curricula marketed for special education cover social, emotional, cognitive and language skills delivered as tablet-mediated games with a supervising adult; they do not perform hands-on daily living skills such as food preparation or grooming.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: commercial robot-delivered special-education lessons. The curricula are limited to social/language targets and the immobile upper-body robot cannot demonstrate or physically prompt hygiene, safety or cooking routines, so it does not transfer.

sources.title: 1X Neo is a $20,000 home robot that will learn chores via teleoperation
sources.claim: General-purpose humanoid robots intended for household chores such as kitchen work still depend on human teleoperators for complex tasks as of late 2025, indicating no autonomous robot performs the cooking/cleaning demonstrations a life-skills lesson requires.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous manipulation of everyday kitchen and household items. Even this precursor capability, needed to model food preparation for students, is not yet autonomous, reinforcing that the instructional task cannot be completed by a robot.

tasks.label: Instruct and monitor students in the use and care of equipment and materials to prevent injuries and damage.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Self-contained or resource special-education classroom, grades 6-8: teacher shows students how to handle and put away everyday classroom materials (scissors, glue guns, staplers, math manipulatives, school-issued Chromebooks/iPads, headphones), states care and safety rules, then circulates while 6-12 students with mixed learning/emotional disabilities work, correcting grips, redirecting rough or unsafe handling, and physically taking or repositioning an item before it is broken or someone is hurt.

Instruction in disability-specific assistive equipment: braillewriter/refreshing braille display and magnifiers, hearing aids and FM/DM systems, AAC speech devices, adapted keyboards, and mobility equipment (walker, gait trainer, wheelchair, white cane). Teacher demonstrates correct handling and daily care/charging/cleaning, uses hand-over-hand or hand-under-hand prompting, and monitors for misuse that could damage costly devices or cause a fall.

Life-skills / functional living lesson in the school's teaching kitchen or laundry area: teacher pre-teaches safe use of knives, stove/oven, microwave, blender, iron and cleaning chemicals, models the steps, then stands within arm's reach of students with intellectual disabilities, prompting and intervening (blocking a hand, turning off a burner, taking a knife) to prevent burns and cuts.

Co-taught or supported inclusion period in a science lab, art room, gym or middle-school CTE/shop class: teacher reviews safety rules and PPE, adapts directions for students with disabilities, and monitors them at lab benches or machines with hot plates, chemicals, kilns, saws or gym apparatus, intervening on unsafe behavior amid a full class of 25-30 students.

Community-based instruction or off-campus work-experience site (grocery store, library, community garden, transit, job-site training): teacher instructs students in using carts, tools, cleaning equipment or fare machines in a setting the school does not control, monitoring for damage to property and injury among the public.

sources.system: CARE autonomous socially assistive robot (Eva/robot tutor)
sources.developer: University research team (Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 2025)
sources.title: CARE: towards customized assistive robot-based education
sources.claim: A socially assistive robot (CARE study) was operated fully autonomously inside a school classroom, adapting learning materials to individual students; its role is conversational tutoring, not handling equipment or supervising students' physical use of tools.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robot-delivered instruction in a school. It shows autonomous verbal/adaptive teaching is possible in a classroom, but the system has no manipulation, no hazard perception over students' hands-on tool use, and no ability to intervene physically, so it does not transfer to instructing and monitoring equipment use to prevent injury or damage.

sources.system: SoftBank Pepper (school wellbeing deployment, Lemaignan et al. 2022)
sources.title: CARE: towards customized assistive robot-based education
sources.claim: A Pepper humanoid was left to operate autonomously ... a school corridor with students diagnosed with autism, interacting socially; the deployment involved conversation and presence only, with no supervision of equipment or physical intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous social robot interaction with students with disabilities inside a school. Establishes that an institution-controlled school (E2) is a feasible robot environment, but the robot neither handles materials nor monitors safe equipment use, so capability does not carry over to this task.

sources.system: Realbotix M-Series humanoid and Optio AI teaching assistant
sources.title: US firm to deploy humanoid robot teaching assistant in New York schools
sources.claim: The most advanced humanoid entering US K-12 classrooms as of mid-2026 is a conversational teacher's-assistant robot for engagement and tutoring; it is a stationary, non-manipulating platform and is not described as supervising students' handling of equipment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot teaching assistant in a US school classroom. It marks the frontier of classroom robots (conversation and engagement) and shows no manipulation or safety-monitoring capability, so it cannot substantiate completion of instructing and monitoring equipment use.

sources.system: Laboratory Safety Assistant (LSA) framework socially assistive robot
sources.title: Social Robot Assistive Intervention for Science Students to Prevent Laboratory Accidents
sources.claim: Robotic supervision of students' safe use of laboratory equipment exists only as a proposed research framework for detecting unsafe behaviors, not as a deployed system that instructs, monitors and intervenes at teacher quality.
sources.transferJustification: Directly related task: robot monitoring of students to prevent equipment-related injuries. It remains a proposed framework evaluated through design studies, with no evidence of autonomous end-to-end supervision or physical intervention, so it cannot support a positive judgment.

instances.label: End-of-lesson/end-of-day reset of the resource or self-contained classroom: gathering pencils, scissors, glue, math manipulatives, laminated cards, books, headphones and adapted equipment off desks and tables and returning each to its labeled bin, shelf, cubby or cart, in a cluttered room with furniture varying by student needs.

Labeling: producing and affixing labels (typed picture-word labels, student name tags, braille/tactile labels, color codes) onto storage bins, drawers, folder tabs, shelf edges, cubbies and devices so students can locate and return materials independently; labels must be straight, at student eye level, and durable.

Preparing and organizing individualized instructional materials: collating worksheets, task cards and visual supports into per-student folders, binders and task boxes; grouping adapted materials and manipulatives per student for the coming lessons; filing them at the correct station or shelf.

Displaying student work in the classroom: selecting and trimming papers, mounting them on backing paper, and stapling/pinning them to a bulletin board or taping to a wall in an arranged layout with title lettering and border, refreshed every few weeks.

Mounting student work in a hallway display case or corridor bulletin board outside the classroom, including seasonal/theme changes, working on a ladder or step stool in a shared corridor with students and staff passing by.

sources.system: Everyday Robots mobile manipulators with RL-at-Scale (Google)
sources.title: Robotic deep RL at scale: Sorting waste and recyclables with a fleet of robots
sources.claim: A fleet of mobile manipulators was deployed for two years inside Google office buildings, autonomously grasping heterogeneous discarded objects at waste stations and placing them into the correct bins, sorting about 84% of objects correctly.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: waste/recycling sorting. It is the same physical operation as classroom put-away — visually identifying varied everyday objects on a surface, grasping them, and placing each into a designated labeled receptacle — performed in an institution-controlled human work building (E2), so it transfers to returning classroom items to labeled bins.

sources.title: Restocking robots deployed in 300 Japanese convenience stores - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Rail-mounted store robots autonomously restock refrigerated beverage shelves in hundreds of FamilyMart convenience stores under a commercial service contract, with remote human takeover only for rare errors.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: shelf replenishment. Placing items into their correct position on shelves against a pre-registered shelf layout is the same operation as returning classroom materials to assigned shelf/bin locations, and it is done inside a human retail facility (E2) with only occasional remote assistance.

sources.title: π0.5: A VLA with Open-World Generalization
sources.claim: A vision-language-action model let mobile manipulators clean up kitchens and bedrooms in homes never seen in training, autonomously putting items away in drawers and cabinets, though the developer states the model is far from perfect.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: tidying/putting items away in an unseen room. Same object class (everyday small handheld objects), same precision (place into an open container or drawer), in a harder, uncontrolled setting; supports the classroom put-away instance at E2 and below.

sources.title: Figure humanoid robots organize room, hang clothes, and make bed without humans
sources.claim: Two humanoids running an onboard learned policy autonomously reset a staged bedroom in under two minutes, organizing loose items, hanging a coat, putting headphones away and making the bed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: room reset/tidying. Comparable to classroom material put-away in object variety and placement precision; shows whole-room autonomous organizing, supporting the put-away instance at structured-facility level.

sources.system: TOPPAN Robot Labeler (robot-arm print-and-apply SCM labeling)
sources.title: Robot Labeler | TOPPAN Infomedia Inc.
sources.claim: Commercial robot-arm labeling systems print and automatically apply adhesive labels at taught positions on packages, cartons and containers moving through a production line, with vision inspection of the applied label.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: industrial print-and-apply labeling. The physical act is identical to labeling storage bins and folders — peel an adhesive paper label and press it squarely onto a taught location on a container — at equal or better precision, in a purpose-built line cell (E1).

sources.title: REA LABEL Robotic Labeler
sources.claim: A second commercial print-and-apply robotic labeler applies printed labels to pallets and products as a fully automatic industrial system.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic label application. Confirms that printing a label and affixing it accurately to a designated surface is a mature, commercially deployed robotic capability in purpose-built cells (E1).

sources.system: Comau robotic palletizing and sheet handling system
sources.title: Robotic Palletizing and Sheet Handling for Pet Food Packaging - Comau
sources.claim: A turnkey robotic palletizing cell handles limp paper slip sheets along with sacks and pallets using a custom multipurpose gripper.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: single-sheet paper pick-and-place in a fixtured cell. Displaying student work requires picking limp paper sheets from a stack and placing them accurately on a surface; combined with robotic label/adhesive application this substantiates the E1 counterfactual (board and sheets fixtured and presented to the machine).

sources.title: Amazon introduces Sparrow—a state-of-the-art robot that handles millions of diverse products
sources.claim: A commercially deployed robotic arm in Amazon fulfillment centers detects, selects and handles individual items from mixed inventory, moving them between totes; it can manipulate about 65% of Amazon's sortable inventory.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: each-picking and kitting of heterogeneous goods into destination totes inside a fenced cell. Comparable to assembling per-student material sets when items are presented in totes at a purpose-built station (E1).

sources.system: Automated book return and sorting system (library AMH)
sources.developer: Library AMH vendors (installation reported by City of Abilene Main Library)
sources.title: Main Library Introduces Automated Book Return • Abilene, TX
sources.claim: Deployed library automated materials handling systems move returned items on a conveyor, identify them by RFID and sort them automatically into designated bins for shelving.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sorting educational materials (books/media) into designated destination bins. Same object class as classroom books and folders; substantiates the E1 counterfactual where materials are brought to a purpose-built sorting machine.

tasks.label: Perform administrative duties, such as school library assistance, hall and cafeteria monitoring, and bus loading and unloading.

instances.label: Hall/passing-period duty: the special ed teacher stands post in a middle school corridor for 4-6 minute passing periods, greeting and redirecting students, enforcing pass/phone/no-running rules, separating horseplay or a shoving conflict, prompting and escorting students with disabilities to their next class, and radioing or responding to a student in behavioral crisis.

Cafeteria duty during lunch waves: supervising 100-200 middle schoolers in a noisy lunchroom, watching students with disabilities for allergy/choking risk, opening packages, carrying or steadying trays, cueing peer interaction, intervening in conflicts, wiping spills, and dismissing tables in order.

Bus loading/unloading duty at arrival and dismissal in the bus loop: escorting a group of students with disabilities out to the correct bus, operating/assisting the wheelchair lift and handing off securement to the driver, checking rosters and dismissal changes, calming or holding back students amid moving buses, in rain, cold, or heat.

School library/media center coverage during a period: supervising students working there, helping students locate materials and use the catalog, staffing circulation checkout/check-in, and shelving carts while students are present.

Back-of-house materials work in the library with no students present (planning period or after hours): processing a bin of returned books, checking them in, sorting them by location, and returning them to storage/shelves; periodic shelf-reading/inventory.

Other duty coverage: morning entrance/arrival supervision, study hall or in-school-suspension proctoring, restroom and locker-area checks, escorting a class to an assembly or through a fire/lockdown drill.

sources.system: Team 1st Technologies / SMP Robotics autonomous security robot
sources.title: Autonomous Security Robots Are Starting to Patrol Schools and Cities, Despite Controversies - The Debrief
sources.claim: An autonomous wheeled security robot pilots at a US high school, patrolling premises and streaming camera feeds to human security officers; it provides surveillance presence but human officers do the responding.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: campus security patrol. It shares the setting (school corridors and grounds) with hall/cafeteria monitoring, but delivers only camera coverage relayed to humans; it does not redirect students, enforce rules, physically intervene, or assist students with disabilities, so it does not transfer to a teacher's supervision duty.

sources.system: bookBot (Dematic ASRS) at the James B. Hunt Jr. Library
sources.title: 'Connecting the Bots': NCSU's 'Book Bot' is part librarian, part robot
sources.claim: A robotic automated storage and retrieval system stores and retrieves library books in a purpose-built climate-controlled vault, delivering requested items within minutes, in daily university-library operation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: library book storage and retrieval. Objects (books) and precision required are identical to reshelving returned materials, and the system runs unattended in a purpose-built robotic vault, which is exactly the E1 counterfactual for back-of-house materials work.

sources.title: North Carolina State University bookBot - Library Technology Guides
sources.claim: The same system stores up to two million items and delivers any requested item within five minutes of an online request.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: retrieving and restoring library materials on request, matching the check-in/return-to-storage portion of library assistance when the work is brought to the machine.

sources.title: Materials on Hand | Materials Handling | Library Journal
sources.claim: Automated materials handling sorters are installed and in routine use in public libraries, automatically checking in and sorting returned items into bins by destination.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated check-in and sorting of returned library materials. Same objects and accuracy requirement as processing a returns bin; the conveyor/sorter is a purpose-built machine environment (E1).

sources.title: DTW adds Whill autonomous wheelchairs to McNamara Terminal | Crain's Detroit Business
sources.claim: Self-driving wheelchairs autonomously transport mobility-impaired passengers along pre-mapped routes inside airport terminals, with over 100 units deployed across US airports.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomously moving a mobility-impaired person through a structured facility. It covers only self-directed point-to-point transport of a cooperative adult on fixed routes; it does not supervise a group of children, verify bus assignments, operate a lift, or hand off to a driver, so it does not complete bus loading duty.

sources.system: Q'STRAINT QUANTUM automatic wheelchair securement station
sources.title: Q'Straint Introduces Revolutionary New Fully Automatic Wheelchair Securement System - School Transportation News
sources.claim: A fully automatic wheelchair securement station lets a wheelchair passenger secure their own chair on a bus at the push of a ..., without driver assistance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: securing a wheelchair inside a bus. It automates one sub-step of bus loading for an independent passenger, but the teacher's duty (escorting students from class, roster checks, behavior management, lift assistance for dependent students) is untouched.

tasks.label: Select, store, order, issue, and inventory classroom equipment, materials, and supplies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-class distribution and collection of instructional materials during a lesson in a middle school resource room or co-taught classroom: passing out worksheets, manipulatives, adapted tools (pencil grips, slant boards, large-print or braille pages, communication boards) matched to each student's accommodations, prompting students in their use, then collecting items and returning them to student bins/cubbies. 6-15 students with disabilities plus paraprofessionals present; layout crowded and shifting.

Issuing durable equipment to individual students and taking it back: Chromebooks/tablets, talking calculators, AAC devices, FM/hearing systems, magnifiers, braille writers. Teacher checks the device out to a named student, logs it, later collects, charges, and re-stores it. Occurs at the start/end of terms and ad hoc through the year in classroom or resource room.

Receiving and putting away supply deliveries and restocking storage: opening boxes of paper, folders, consumables, laminating film, adapted materials and curriculum kits; shelving them in classroom cabinets, a supply closet or storeroom; sorting into labeled bins; keeping the storage area orderly. Mixed small items of varied shape, doors and tight aisles, done between classes or after school.

Pulling and prepping materials before lessons and putting them back after: gathering manipulatives, sensory items, laminated card sets, per-student folders and bins from cabinets and the resource room, loading a cart, carrying them to general-education classrooms or therapy spaces, then returning and re-storing everything at day's end.

Periodic inventory: counting consumables and durable equipment (assistive tech devices, textbooks, curriculum kits, math manipulative sets), checking condition and charge, reconciling against the district asset/inventory list, and recording counts and discrepancies in a spreadsheet or district system. Done in classroom cabinets and the storeroom, typically at term start/end or for annual asset audits.

Selecting and ordering: reviewing vendor catalogs/sites and the classroom or IEP budget, deciding which curricula, adapted materials and equipment fit particular students' IEP goals and sensory/physical needs, checking what is already on hand in the closet, then submitting requisitions to the school or district and following up when goods arrive.

sources.title: Amazon's Vulcan robot uses force sensing to stow items
sources.claim: Amazon's Vulcan robot autonomously picks and stows a large majority of the varied small items in its fulfillment centers into shelf bins at speeds comparable to human ..., in purpose-built stow stations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: warehouse stowing/replenishment. Placing diverse small consumer goods into designated shelf bins is the same physical operation as putting away delivered classroom supplies into labeled bins and shelves, with comparable object variety and precision; it is demonstrated only where items are presented in totes at a fixtured station.

sources.title: Staples deploys RightHand Robotics tech in its fulfillment centers
sources.claim: Autonomous piece-picking arms deployed across Staples' North American fulfillment centers pick individual office/school supply items of varied shape, size and packaging to fill orders.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: each-picking/kitting of office supplies. Assembling a set of specified small items (pens, folders, notebooks, kits) from stock is the same operation as pulling a list of classroom materials for a lesson or per-student bin, on identical object classes, when stock is presented to the machine.

sources.title: UPS deploys Verity warehouse drones for inventory tracking
sources.claim: Verity's autonomous inventory drones fly warehouse aisles unattended to count and verify stock and flag discrepancies, deployed at UPS Supply Chain Solutions and Maersk facilities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated cycle counting. Scanning stored goods, counting them and reconciling against the inventory record is the same operation as inventorying classroom equipment and supplies, provided items sit on tagged, machine-readable racking as a purpose-built setting would present them.

sources.title: BJ's to roll out inventory robots chainwide
sources.claim: Simbe's Tally robots autonomously roam grocery and club-store aisles imaging shelves to track stock levels and location, deployed chainwide at BJ's Wholesale Club and other grocers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: retail shelf auditing. It shows autonomous stock counting inside an institution-controlled human facility, but it depends on planogrammed, barcoded, open-faced shelving rather than closed classroom cabinets and unlabeled bins.

sources.title: Diligent Robotics completes 300,000 pharmacy deliveries with Moxi
sources.claim: Moxi mobile manipulators run autonomously in more than 30 US hospitals, fetching and delivering medications, lab specimens, supplies and equipment along corridors and elevators built for people.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: intra-facility supply transport. Moving requested supplies from a storeroom to a work area within a human-occupied institution is the transport half of pulling materials to a classroom; it does not cover picking diverse adapted materials out of classroom cabinets.

sources.title: How Diligent's Robots Are Making a Difference in Texas Hospitals
sources.claim: Moxi performs commercial mobile manipulation in hospitals, retrieving supply items from supply closets and delivering them ... without human control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hospital supply fetching. Retrieving named items from an institutional storage room and bringing them to the point of use parallels pulling classroom materials, but the demonstrated items are standardized clinical supplies in uniform bins, not the mixed, unlabelled contents of a special-education cabinet.

sources.title: Libraries turn to laptop vending machines to fulfill students' late night studying needs
sources.claim: Automated device-dispensing kiosks issue laptops/Chromebooks to individual students on ID authentication and accept and recharge returns unattended; they are sold to and installed in schools, campus libraries and other institutions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: unattended device lending. Issuing a specific device to an identified student, logging the loan, and taking the item back for charging is the same transaction as a teacher checking equipment out to students, executed with the stock fixtured in purpose-built bays.

sources.system: BD Rowa Vmax 160 robotic dispensing system
sources.title: Enhancing Operational Efficiency and Service Delivery through a Robotic Dispensing System: A Case Study from a Retail Pharmacy in Brazil
sources.claim: A robotic storage-and-dispensing system installed in a pharmacy stores packs and retrieves and dispenses them automatically on request, cutting dispensing time versus manual handling.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated stock storage and on-demand issue. Storing incoming units and issuing a requested unit to a person at a service point mirrors storing supplies and issuing equipment, but only inside a machine-built stockroom, not on open classroom shelving.

tasks.label: Provide assistive devices, supportive technology, and assistance accessing facilities, such as restrooms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In a middle-school classroom or resource room, the teacher gets a student's supportive technology working for the lesson: mounting a speech-generating AAC device on a wheelchair tray and positioning the switch, pairing an FM/DM transmitter to a student's hearing aids/cochlear implant, waking and configuring a text-to-speech tablet or braille display, and troubleshooting when a device drops its Bluetooth link or loses charge mid-period. Output accepted only when the individual student can actually operate the device.

Restroom access and personal care for a student with physical or intellectual disability: taking the student to the accessible restroom on a schedule or on request, transferring from wheelchair to toilet (with or without a lift/gait belt), managing clothing and briefs, cleanup and handwashing, watching for skin/health issues, all while preserving dignity and privacy and following the IEP/health-care plan.

Fitting and adjusting adaptive equipment on or around the student's body: repositioning a student in an adapted chair with lateral supports and pelvic straps, setting up a stander or slant board, putting on a weighted vest, hand splint or pencil grip, adjusting footplates and tray height, and re-checking posture through the period.

Walking escort and physical mobility support to facilities: guiding a student who is blind along a hallway route to the restroom or cafeteria, steadying a student using a walker or gait belt on stairs and thresholds, and supervising a student with behavioral or seizure risk through a crowded passing period, carrying the student's device along.

Conveying a seated student who can sit and transfer independently along familiar indoor routes inside the school building — classroom to restroom door, cafeteria, elevator, therapy room or bus loop — pushing or accompanying the wheelchair, holding doors, and returning the student to class.

Courier work with equipment: fetching a charged AAC device, FM transmitter, laptop or adapted materials from the charging cart/resource room, carrying it across the building to the general-education classroom where the student is, and collecting and re-docking equipment at the end of the day.

sources.date: 2025-04-14 (Detroit launch; earlier deployments at LAX, MIA, SEA, AMS, YWG)
sources.title: Unifi Aviation Launches WHILL Autonomous Wheelchair Service at Detroit Metro Airport
sources.claim: WHILL's autonomous power wheelchairs are in commercial service at multiple airports, autonomously conveying seated passengers along pre-mapped routes through busy terminals and returning to base unoccupied.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: conveying a seated person who can transfer independently along a mapped indoor route inside an institutional building shared with pedestrians. This is the same physical act as wheeling a student from classroom to restroom door or cafeteria in a school corridor — same payload (a seated person), same speeds, same obstacle-avoidance demands.

sources.system: Relay / RelayRx delivery robots at BayCare hospitals
sources.title: BayCare Expands Autonomous Hospital Delivery with New Relay Robots at Winter Haven Hospitals
sources.claim: Relay delivery robots run autonomously inside hospitals, riding elevators, opening badge-access doors and threading hallway traffic to carry items between departments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: intra-building courier delivery of small portable items in a staffed institution. A school building's corridors, elevators and secured doors are the same class of environment, and a charged tablet, FM transmitter or set of adapted materials is the same class of payload as the lab specimens and supplies Relay carries.

sources.title: Diligent Robotics hits 1M picks with Moxi robot in healthcare settings
sources.claim: Diligent Robotics' Moxi, a mobile manipulator with an arm, is deployed across dozens of US hospitals doing fetch-and-deliver runs, including autonomous elevator rides, at fleet scale.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous mobile manipulation for fetch-and-deliver of portable items through corridors and elevators in a human-occupied institutional facility, the same courier function a special-education teacher performs when moving devices between the resource room and classrooms.

sources.title: The strong robot with the gentle touch | RIKEN
sources.claim: Robots that lift and transfer a person between bed and wheelchair remain experimental and operator-controlled; ROBEAR was a research prototype and was never commercialized.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: caregiver transfer of a person between wheelchair and another surface — the physical core of restroom/toileting assistance. Cited only as context for a negative judgment: the machine is caregiver-operated and experimental, so it cannot substantiate autonomous completion.

sources.system: physically assistive mobile and manipulator robots (survey of the field)
sources.developer: Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems (Nanavati, Ranganeni, Cakmak)
sources.title: Physically Assistive Robots: A Systematic Review of Mobile and Manipulator Robots That Physically Assist People with Disabilities
sources.claim: A 2024 systematic review of physically assistive robots for people with disabilities (ambulating, dressing, personal hygiene) characterizes the field as recent research with end-to-end systems only now reaching real-world user studies.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic assistance with activities of daily living (hygiene, dressing, positioning) for people with disabilities — the same acts a special-education teacher performs. Used only as context for negative judgments; autonomy of individual systems is not established here.

sources.title: The Xiaoban robot toilet comes to you, not the other way around
sources.claim: An autonomous self-driving robot toilet (Xiaoban) was shown at a 2026 aged-care expo; it navigates to a user and self-cleans, but the user must get onto it and it has no capability to transfer, undress or clean a person.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: bringing toilet facilities to a mobility-impaired person. It bears on restroom-access assistance but does not perform the transfer, clothing management or hygiene supervision that the school instance requires, so it supports no positive judgment.

tasks.label: Organize and supervise games and other recreational activities to promote physical, mental, and social development.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-group game session in the special education classroom: teacher sets out a board/card game, cooperative task, or social-skills game for 3-8 middle schoolers with autism, ADHD, emotional disturbance or intellectual disability; explains and adapts rules, assigns turns, redirects off-task or escalating behavior, resolves disputes, prompts peer interaction, and cleans up. Students vary in communication level; some are nonverbal or use AAC devices.

Adapted physical education / gym or multipurpose-room games: teacher hauls out and arranges cones, balls, mats, scooters, parachute; demonstrates and modifies activities (relay races, modified basketball, bowling) for students with mobility aids, wheelchairs, or visual impairment; provides hand-over-hand or physical support, referees, keeps students safe from collisions and equipment, and stows gear afterwards.

Recess or outdoor break on school grounds: teacher/para escorts the group outside, organizes an informal game (kickball, tag, walking club) on blacktop or field, monitors a scattered group among general-education peers, watches for elopement, bullying, falls and sensory overload, intervenes physically when needed, and lines students up to return to class.

One-on-one seated leisure/social-skills session at a table with a single student: teacher runs a structured turn-taking game (cards, board game, matching or tablet game) to build attention, turn-taking, winning/losing tolerance and conversation, using prompting hierarchies and reinforcement, and records IEP goal data.

Community-based or off-campus recreation: bowling alley, community park, YMCA, Special Olympics practice or field day; teacher transports/escorts students, negotiates unfamiliar layout and crowds, sets up adapted equipment, supervises safety and social behavior in public, and manages transitions.

sources.system: Jibo social robot (Yale, Scassellati et al.)
sources.title: Improving social skills in children with ASD using a long-term, in-home social robot | Science Robotics
sources.claim: The autonomous tabletop social robot Jibo delivered daily 30-minute social-skills game sessions to 12 children with ASD aged 6-12 in their homes for one month, with the child and a caregiver, producing measurable social communication gains; content was prespecified.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led structured social-skills game sessions with children with disabilities. It maps onto the one-on-one seated game instance (same population type, same purpose of promoting social/mental development through a game), though the activities are tablet/story based rather than physical games and a caregiver is always present.

sources.developer: University of Hertfordshire (Wainer, Robins, Dautenhahn et al.)
sources.title: Using the Humanoid Robot KASPAR to Autonomously Play Triadic Games and Facilitate Collaborative Play Among Children With Autism (IEEE TAMD)
sources.claim: The humanoid robot KASPAR ran a collaborative imitation game with pairs of children with autism fully autonomously, sensing game state and child behavior to prompt, encourage and advise the players.
sources.transferJustification: Directly related: the robot organizes and moderates a structured game with children with disabilities to promote social development, at a fixed instrumented game station with the game pre-set for the robot.

sources.developer: academic HRI group (Int. Journal of Artificial Life Research study)
sources.title: An Autonomous Robot-to-Group Exercise Coach at a Senior Living Community: A Study in Human-Robot Interaction
sources.claim: A NAO humanoid was programmed as an autonomous group exercise instructor at a senior ..., directing warm-up and exercise routines for a group of residents.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: leading a group physical activity session in an institutional facility. Transfer to adapted PE with middle-school students is weak: the robot only demonstrates seated/standing movements to cooperative adults, and does not handle, set up or stow equipment, referee, or provide the safety supervision and physical assistance that students with disabilities require.

sources.title: GoBot Go! Using a Custom Assistive Robot to Promote Physical Activity in Children (Oregon State University)
sources.claim: GoBot, a custom child-sized mobile robot, increased toddlers' physical activity through interactive keep-away play in a study room; it runs either teleoperated or on a pre-programmed semi-autonomous routine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: eliciting children's physical activity through robot-mediated play. Control is teleoperation or a scripted routine, and the robot neither organizes an activity for a group nor supervises safety, so it cannot substantiate completion of the PE or recess instances.

sources.title: Robot named 'Milo' helps special needs students in Pendleton South Carolina learn
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo robot is commercially deployed in US school special education programs, delivering social-emotional lessons to students, but sessions are run by a human facilitator using a curriculum and tablet alongside the student.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered social-skills instruction in a school special education classroom. Lesson selection and student supervision remain with the human facilitator, so autonomy is unclear and it cannot support a positive completion judgment.

sources.title: A Humanoid Social Robot as a Teaching Assistant in the Classroom
sources.claim: A 2025 evaluation of humanoid social robots as classroom teaching assistants concludes that current robotic systems are not yet ... for the full range of classroom interaction, working best in face-to-face or small-group settings.
sources.transferJustification: Context on the state of classroom robots; supports the negative judgments on group supervision rather than any positive completion claim.

tasks.label: Visit schools to tutor students with sensory impairments and to consult with teachers regarding students' special needs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Itinerant teacher of the visually impaired travels to a middle school for a scheduled pull-out session with a braille-reading 7th grader: pre-teaching upcoming science/math content, drilling Nemeth code and tactile graphic interpretation, checking the student's braille output, then a 10-minute debrief with the general education teacher about upcoming units and needed adaptations.

Itinerant teacher of the deaf/hard of hearing visits a middle school to tutor a student on academic vocabulary, listening/comprehension strategies, and self-advocacy, then consults with the content-area teachers about seating, classroom acoustics, use of the remote-microphone system, and captioned media.

Consultation-only visit: the itinerant specialist observes the student during a general education class, then meets with the classroom teacher, paraprofessional, and case manager to review accommodations, interpret assessment/IEP progress data, and advise on modifying instructional materials and assessments.

Assistive technology support visit: coaching the student and the classroom teacher on screen reader, braille notetaker/embosser, magnification, or personal FM/DM system use, and verifying that upcoming classroom materials are accessible in the needed format.

Rural or multi-district travel day (or scheduled tele-consultation) covering several schools with brief check-ins: quick student skill checks, teacher questions answered, materials dropped off, and scheduling of follow-up services.

instances.label: Duplicating and finishing print materials for the day's lessons: running copies of differentiated worksheets, modified tests and visual supports on the school workroom copier, collating and stapling packets, laminating and cutting task cards, and filing the sets into period folders/bins.

Reconfiguring the classroom layout for the activity: moving student desks/tables and chairs into rows, pods or station clusters, unstacking and tucking chairs, and clearing pathways so wheelchairs and walkers can reach each station.

Assembling and setting out hands-on materials: filling task boxes and bins with manipulatives, math tools, sorting/vocational items and art/science lab supplies, building one kit per student, and placing a set at each desk or station.

Producing accessible versions of the day's materials for students with sensory impairments: embossing braille worksheets, running tactile graphics, and generating enlarged-print copies from the digital lesson files.

Setting up assistive technology and adaptive equipment: charging and pairing AAC devices and tablets, fitting switches and mounts to individual students' wheelchairs, positioning adapted seating, slant boards and standers, and connecting a CCTV/magnifier or amplification system.

Setting up a life-skills or vocational area: laying out ingredients, utensils and appliances in the classroom kitchen for a cooking lesson, or preparing a laundry/cleaning or job-training workstation, and resetting the area afterward.

Preparing the instructional display and posted supports: writing the agenda and objectives on the board, posting the visual schedule, picture supports and anchor charts on walls, and setting up the projector/interactive panel and laptop.

sources.system: Durst P5 Robotics (two KUKA feeding/stacking robots)
sources.title: The P5 Robotics, Durst's 180-degree loading and unloading solution
sources.claim: Durst's P5 Robotics is a commercial print-production cell in which two KUKA arms autonomously pick media from pallets, feed the printer and stack printed output — machine handling of printed sheet material in a purpose-built cell.

It transfers to producing class sets of printed materials because the objects (paper/board stock), the placement precision required, and the fenced production-cell environment are the same.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated kitting of mixed small goods into totes. Classroom material kits (manipulatives, sorting items, supplies) are comparable objects at comparable precision, and the E1 form of the instance presents them in bins exactly as a kitting cell does.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: lifting and repositioning furniture-scale objects (inventory pods) to designated floor positions. Classroom furniture rearrangement at E1 — standardized desks/tables on a machine-legible floor with marked target positions — is the same payload class and placement precision.

sources.title: Amazon unveils first fully autonomous mobile robot

sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomously moving wheeled carts to defined locations. Moving wheeled classroom tables and chair racks into a required layout involves the same object class and positioning tolerance in a floor space prepared for the machine.

sources.title: Braille Printers | American Foundation for the Blind

sources.transferJustification: Related task: general object rearrangement and tidying in as-found rooms. Cited as a negative bound: even the best generalist system is a low-reliability demo, so classroom setup in an occupied school room is not supported.
