instances.label: Setting up assistive/supportive technology on or around the student at the start of a lesson in a secondary classroom: mounting an AAC speech device on a wheelchair tray at the right angle, powering/logging it in, attaching a head switch or eye-gaze unit, fitting headphones, pairing an FM/DM transmitter to a student's hearing aids or cochlear implant, positioning a video magnifier or refreshable braille display, and checking the student can actually activate it, amid 8-15 teenagers.

Fetching and delivering assistive equipment and materials around the school building: bringing a charged loaner Chromebook or AAC device from the AT closet/charging cart to a classroom, carrying braille-embossed handouts from the vision office, dropping a device at the AT specialist's room, collecting devices at day's end for charging. Corridors, elevators, badge-access doors.

Escorting a wheelchair-using student or a blind/low-vision student along building routes to the restroom, elevator, cafeteria, nurse, or bus loop and back - route-finding and safe passage through crowded hallways during passing periods; the student transfers/toilets independently once there.

Hands-on ambulation support en route to a facility: gait belt, steadying a student with ataxia or poor balance, managing a walker or gait trainer, preventing falls, holding heavy fire doors open while physically supporting the student.

Restroom personal-care assistance for a student with significant physical or intellectual disability: wheeling into the accessible stall, transferring from chair to toilet (manually or with a hoist/sling), managing clothing and braces, toileting hygiene, catheter or brief/diaper change, cleanup, handwashing, re-transfer and repositioning.

Off-campus community-based instruction or field trip: assisting a student to access restrooms and facilities in an unfamiliar store, worksite or transit station - non-compliant doors, curbs, cluttered aisles, crowded public restrooms - and setting up the student's device (communication board, tablet) in the field.

sources.title: How Diligent's Robots Are Making a Difference in Texas Hospitals - IEEE Spectrum
sources.claim: Moxi, an autonomous mobile manipulator, picks supplies out of supply closets ... delivers them to rooms in hospital buildings, navigating corridors, doors and elevators without an operator.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: intra-building fetch-and-delivery of small equipment and supplies. Transfers to delivering assistive devices, chargers and braille-printed materials between rooms of a school: same object class (handheld items/totes), same corridor-and-elevator environment, same hand-off-to-a-person endpoint.

sources.title: Serve Robotics to Acquire Diligent Robotics, Expanding Physical AI Platform Beyond the Sidewalk
sources.claim: Moxi is commercially deployed at scale in US hospitals with over a million completed autonomous deliveries, establishing worker-level reliability for item transport inside an institutional building.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (institutional item delivery); this item establishes deployment scale and reliability rather than a new capability.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: escorting a seated person with impaired mobility along building routes among crowds. Transfers to taking a wheelchair-using student down a school corridor to the restroom or cafeteria: same payload (a seated person), same indoor institutional floor plan, same pedestrian traffic.

sources.transferJustification: Cited only to document the state of the art for the restroom personal-care instance; it is a demo with unclear autonomy and cannot support a positive judgment.

tasks.label: Instruct students in daily living skills required for independent maintenance and self-sufficiency, such as hygiene, safety, and food preparation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Life-skills kitchen lesson in a high school functional-skills classroom: teacher models and then guides 3-8 students with intellectual/developmental disabilities through a task-analyzed recipe (sandwich, microwave meal, stovetop item) — demonstrating knife use, spreading, measuring, appliance operation; delivering graduated prompts including hand-over-hand physical prompts; intervening physically for burn/cut safety; supervising cleanup and taking IEP data.

Personal hygiene and grooming instruction in a school restroom or hygiene/changing area: teacher demonstrates and prompts handwashing, toothbrushing, deodorant/face care, hair brushing, shower/locker routines after PE, and menstrual hygiene for individual students with moderate to severe disabilities, using modeling, physical guidance, and dignity/privacy management.

Classroom-based safety instruction lesson: teacher leads a small group through fire/kitchen safety, medication and household chemical safety, street crossing, stranger and online safety, using visual supports, role play with props, simulated scenarios, and comprehension checks; manages behavior and adapts to varied communication levels.

Community-based instruction off campus: teacher takes 2-6 students to a grocery store, laundromat, restaurant, or transit stop and teaches shopping, ordering, money handling, and travel safety in situ, with in-the-moment prompting, safety supervision in crowds and traffic, and generalization data collection.

School 'apartment' / domestic-skills lab session: teacher instructs students in laundry (sorting, machine operation), bed making, table setting, dish washing, and basic housekeeping, demonstrating each step and fading prompts across repeated sessions.

sources.date: 2016 (case study); product still marketed in schools through 2025
sources.title: IESD Case Study: Children on the Autism Spectrum Show Improvement with robots4autism (Spartanburg)
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo robot delivers a social-emotional/autism curriculum in school special-education pull-out sessions, but sessions are run by a human facilitator who controls the lesson from a tablet; the robot performs no object manipulation or physical prompting of the student.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-mediated special-education instruction in a school. It is the closest deployed analogue to the rated task, but it covers only spoken/expressive social-skills lessons under continuous facilitator control, with no demonstration of kitchen, hygiene, or safety task performance and no physical prompting, so capability does not transfer to daily-living-skills instruction.

sources.developer: AMMACHI Labs, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham with University of Glasgow
sources.title: Handwashing robot helps schoolkids make a clean break with bad habits — University of Glasgow news
sources.claim: The 'Pepe' social robot installed at a school handwashing station in Kerala coached children's handwashing and increased handwashing duration/frequency, but the researchers state the robot was not yet able to interact autonomously without human input.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered hygiene coaching at a school washbasin. It targets the same skill domain (handwashing) in a school, but it is a prompting/encouragement device for typically developing primary pupils, is not established as autonomous, and does not perform the individualized prompting, fading, and progress measurement a special educator's hygiene instruction requires.

sources.system: Handwashing action detection system for social robot (Pepe platform)
sources.title: Handwashing Action Detection System for an Autonomous Social Robot (arXiv 2210.15804)
sources.claim: Follow-on work presents a vision-based handwashing action recognition module intended for an autonomous social robot that observes and gives feedback on children's handwashing; it is a perception component evaluated on video, not a fielded instructional robot.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated observation and feedback on a hygiene routine. Even taken at face value it supplies only step recognition and verbal feedback for one routine; it does not model the skill, deliver physical prompts, or handle the grooming, toileting, and dignity components of secondary special-education hygiene instruction.

sources.developer: SoftBank Robotics / Robotlab, used by university researchers

sources.claim: A NAO humanoid has been used to deliver a scripted classroom lesson autonomously (including slide control) to 11-12 year old mainstream students in research trials, with the teacher present.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous delivery of a pre-scripted classroom lesson. It shows verbal lesson playback in a school, but it is a fixed script for typically developing students with a teacher supervising; it does not include demonstration with real materials, individualized prompt hierarchies, behavior management, or safety supervision required here.

sources.title: Miso Robotics' Flippy Fry Station robot surpasses 5M baskets — Fast Casual
sources.claim: Miso Robotics' Flippy Fry Station autonomously performs a fixed food-preparation job (basket loading, frying, dumping) in commercial quick-service kitchens at scale.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous food preparation in a structured kitchen. It shows a machine can execute one narrowly fixtured cooking step, but the rated instance is teaching a student to cook — modeling, graduated physical prompting, error correction, and safety supervision of a person — none of which this single-purpose fry arm performs.

tasks.label: Plan and supervise class projects, field trips, visits by guest speakers, or other experiential activities, and guide students in learning from those activities.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multi-session hands-on class project in a secondary special education classroom (e.g., science model, poster/display, group art or STEM build) for 8-15 students with mixed learning, emotional and intellectual disabilities plus paraprofessionals: teacher plans the project against IEP goals, procures and sets out materials and adapted tools, demonstrates steps, circulates giving verbal, gestural and hand-over-hand prompts, manages scissors/glue-gun/tool safety and behavior escalations, adapts materials on the fly, then leads a debrief tying the activity to learning objectives.

Community-based instruction field trip: teacher plans logistics (site contact, permission slips, bus, staffing ratios, medical/behavior plans, adapted schedules), then escorts 6-12 students with disabilities on public sidewalks, transit or a bus to a grocery store, restaurant, museum or civic office; supervises safety in traffic and crowds, keeps track of students who may elope, prompts functional skills (money, ordering, wayfinding), handles unexpected behavior or medical events, and runs a classroom debrief afterward.

Guest speaker or in-school experiential event (employer, self-advocate, first responder, transition-agency representative): teacher recruits and schedules the speaker, prepares students with pre-written questions and visual supports, sets up the room, AV, accessible seating and interpreter/captioning, hosts and moderates the session while monitoring attention and behavior, and guides a follow-up reflection activity.

On-campus vocational/life-skills experiential activity (school kitchen or coffee cart, school store, greenhouse, laundry, horticulture or shop area): teacher plans and sets up task stations and job aids, demonstrates equipment use (oven, register, mixer, tools), supervises students performing the work with prompting and fading, enforces safety, collects IEP data, and debriefs performance with students.

Work-based learning visit at a community employer site with a small group (2-4 students): teacher coordinates with the site supervisor, orients students to the tasks and workplace rules, job-coaches with modeling and physical prompting, monitors safety and productivity, troubleshoots problems with the employer, records data, and debriefs students on what was learned.

sources.title: A Humanoid Social Robot as a Teaching Assistant in the Classroom
sources.claim: A humanoid social robot (Pepper) linked to an LLM was tested in a high school classroom presenting new learning content to groups ...; this is content delivery in a research trial, not planning or supervising a hands-on project or trip.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = delivering instructional content in a secondary classroom. It shares the setting (E2 school classroom) but not the demands of this task: no planning/logistics, no handling or setup of project materials, no custodial safety supervision, no individualized physical prompting.

sources.title: Robots For Autism Teach Human Emotion
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo is a commercially deployed special-education robot used in hundreds of US schools, but it delivers pre-authored social-skills lessons to one or a few students rather than supervising projects, trips or events.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = robot-delivered instruction to students with disabilities in a special education classroom. It does not transfer: Milo is stationary, session-based and adult-run, and does not plan activities, prepare materials, or supervise groups.

sources.title: Can Robots Help Autistic Children Better Their Academic Performance?
sources.claim: Milo sessions require a human facilitator who selects and runs each lesson from an iPad while sitting with the students, so the robot is not operating autonomously as a supervising adult.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (robot-delivered special education lessons); cited to establish the human-in-the-loop control that disqualifies it as autonomous supervision.

It does not transfer: the robot has no custody or safety responsibility for minors with disabilities, cannot manage behavior or elopement, cannot plan trip logistics, and does no hands-on material setup or individualized prompting.

tasks.label: Provide additional instruction in vocational areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Classroom-based pre-vocational instruction reteaching: in a high school resource room, the teacher gives a small group of students with learning or emotional disabilities extra instruction on job applications, resumes, interviewing, workplace expectations and safety rules, using worksheets, discussion, role-play and checks for understanding.

Hands-on vocational skills lab inside the school (school kitchen, coffee cart, laundry, school store, custodial route, horticulture): the teacher breaks a job into task-analysis steps, models each step, prompts and fades prompts, and gives corrective feedback to students with intellectual disabilities or autism.

Community-based work-site instruction: the teacher accompanies two to four transition-age students to a local employer (grocery store, hotel housekeeping, nursing home, warehouse), teaches the employer's task sequence on site, coaches on pace, quality and coworker interaction, and collects data on independence.

One-on-one supplemental instruction with disability-specific adaptations: e.g., teaching a blind student screen-reader and braille-notetaker workflows for office tasks, or a deaf student the signed vocabulary and visual supports needed for a shop or food-service job, re-teaching content missed in the general CTE setting.

Push-in support within a career and technical education course (auto shop, welding, cosmetology, building trades): the special education teacher provides modified explanations, adapted step guides, and extra practice alongside the CTE instructor so the student can meet course competencies safely.

tasks.label: Instruct and monitor students in the use and care of equipment and materials to prevent injuries and damage.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Life-skills/functional classroom (self-contained, students with intellectual or multiple disabilities): teacher demonstrates and supervises use of kitchen appliances (microwave, stove, knives), cleaning and laundry equipment; provides gestural and hand-over-hand physical prompting, blocks unsafe actions (burns, cuts), and runs the put-away/clean-and-care routine at the end of the period.

Assistive/adaptive equipment instruction for students who are blind, deaf, or physically disabled: teaching operation and daily care of braille notetakers, video magnifiers, white canes, hearing aids and FM/DM systems, AAC speech devices, walkers and manual/power wheelchairs; physically positioning devices, checking charging, cleaning, and monitoring safe use during the school day.

Co-taught or inclusion setting in a general-education science lab, art room, or CTE/shop class: special educator circulates with the students on her caseload, restates and demonstrates safety procedures for glassware, hot plates, chemicals, sewing machines or hand/power tools, checks PPE, and intervenes physically when a student mishandles equipment.

Resource room or self-contained academic class with 1:1 devices: instructing students in careful handling, charging, transport and storage of Chromebooks/tablets, headphones, calculators, and manipulatives; monitoring the group to prevent dropped or damaged devices and correcting rough handling on the spot.

Community-based instruction / work-based learning off campus (grocery store, warehouse, restaurant, transit): teaching and supervising students' use of carts, dish machines, box cutters, POS terminals, cleaning chemicals and public transit equipment in a workplace or public setting taken as found.

sources.title: RoboKind - EdTech Digest
sources.claim: RoboKind's Milo, the most widely adopted commercial classroom robot in US special education, delivers a scripted social-emotional/communication curriculum in short pull-out sessions with a facilitator; it does not instruct students in equipment use or supervise equipment handling, and has no manipulator to intervene physically.
sources.transferJustification: Closest commercially deployed robot in secondary special-education classrooms; cited to show the scope of deployed classroom robots (social-skills delivery only), not to substantiate completion of equipment instruction or safety monitoring.

sources.system: Laboratory Safety Assistant (LSA) framework, socially assistive robot
sources.title: Socially Assistive Robot as Laboratory Safety Assistant for Science Students (IEEE Xplore)
sources.claim: A socially assistive 'Laboratory Safety Assistant' robot framework for detecting unsafe student behavior in science labs exists only as a research/participatory-design prototype that flags guideline violations (missing goggles or gloves) for the teacher; it does not teach equipment use or physically prevent injury.
sources.transferJustification: Directly related sub-function (monitoring students to prevent laboratory injuries and damage); cited because it is the nearest robotic attempt, but it is a prototype detection/alerting aid dependent on a human supervisor, so it does not substantiate whole-task completion.

sources.system: SoftBank Pepper in a Special Educational Needs school
sources.title: "It's Important to Think of Pepper as a Teaching Aid or Resource External to the Classroom": A Social Robot in a School for Autistic Children
sources.claim: Social robots placed in special-education schools operate as short-term, co-designed teaching aids external to the core classroom routine rather than as supervising instructors.
sources.transferJustification: Same population and setting as the task; shows robots in SEN schools function as supplementary aids under staff supervision, not as instructors who monitor equipment use to prevent injuries.

tasks.label: Provide interpretation and transcription of regular classroom materials through Braille and sign language.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Real-time sign language interpretation (ASL/SEE) of a general-education secondary lecture, discussion, and video for a deaf or hard-of-hearing student: the special educator signs teacher speech, peer comments, and questions, and voices the student's signed contributions, as the class proceeds.

Transcribing print handouts, worksheets, quizzes, and tests into contracted UEB/Nemeth braille ahead of class (formatting per code rules, proofreading) and issuing the braille copy to the student, either as embossed hard copy or as an electronic braille file for a notetaker/refreshable display.

Producing tactile access to graphics for math/science/social studies units: converting graphs, cell diagrams, maps, and geometry figures into tactile graphics (graphics-capable embosser, swell paper, collage or 3D models) with braille labels and a key.

On-the-spot access during class: interpreting or describing what the teacher writes on the board, brailling a pop quiz or last-minute handout, reading back a student's brailled work, and relaying announcements as the lesson unfolds.

Coordinating and preparing longer-form accessible versions of core materials: obtaining publisher files or APH/Bookshare volumes, converting and reformatting textbook chapters and novels into braille or large print, and checking the result against the print original.
Interpretation/transcription outside the regular classroom: assemblies, science labs, field trips, athletics and clubs, standardized testing sessions, and IEP or parent meetings.

tasks.label: Perform administrative duties, such as school library assistance, hall and cafeteria monitoring, and bus loading and unloading.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hall/passing-period duty in a secondary school corridor: standing a post during passing periods, visually scanning a crowded hallway of adolescents, checking passes, verbally redirecting students, breaking up shoving or verbal conflicts, physically escorting a dysregulated student with an emotional disability to a quiet space or the office, opening doors and clearing a path for a student using a wheelchair or a white cane, and doing restroom sweeps.

Cafeteria/lunch duty: supervising several hundred students during a lunch period, circulating between tables, prompting and cueing students on the IEP caseload, opening packaging/carrying trays/assisting with feeding or utensil use for students with physical or intellectual disabilities, intervening in food-throwing or conflicts, wiping spills, and dismissing tables in order.

Bus loading/unloading duty at arrival and dismissal: escorting a group of students with disabilities from classrooms to the outdoor bus loop, matching each student to the correct bus number against a roster, holding students back from moving buses, guiding a wheelchair user onto the lift and handing off to the driver/aide for securement, buckling harnesses or safety vests, and calming students who elope or refuse to board, in rain, snow, or heat.

Other duty-station coverage: study hall or in-school-suspension monitoring, morning entrance/metal-detector and dismissal door duty, supervising students during assemblies, fire drills, and hallway transitions to specials or work-study, and covering an unstaffed classroom or locker-room transition.

School library/media center assistance during a duty period: staffing the circulation desk, checking materials in and out, reshelving returns, helping students locate books and use catalog computers or assistive-tech stations, printing/scanning support, and monitoring student behavior in the media center.

sources.title: Schools & Higher Education | Knightscope
sources.claim: Knightscope's K5 autonomous security robot is marketed and deployed for school campuses, but the described role is patrolling parking lots and structures and recording vehicle/pedestrian traffic — observation and deterrence, not supervising or physically assisting students.
sources.transferJustification: Closest deployed analogue to hall/bus-loop monitoring: a patrolling observer on institution-controlled school grounds. It does not transfer to the task, because the duty requires verbal redirection, physical escort, and hands-on assistance to students, which a camera-mast patrol robot does not perform.

sources.system: Team 1st Technologies / campus security patrol robot (Santa Fe Public Schools pilot)
sources.title: US school turns to AI-driven security robot for additional surveillance measures | IFSEC Insider
sources.claim: A Santa Fe, New Mexico school piloted an AI-enabled security robot that patrols campus grounds 24/7 and streams 360-degree camera footage to human security staff, who remain the responders.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (campus security patrol) in the same setting as hall and bus-loop duty; it substantiates only autonomous navigation and video capture, with humans handling every interaction with people, so it does not carry over to monitoring duties that require intervention.

sources.title: Cobalt intelligent indoor security robot | Security Info Watch
sources.claim: Cobalt's indoor security robot autonomously patrols indoor human workplaces, but whenever a person must be interacted with or an anomaly handled, a remote human specialist pilots the robot and speaks through it.
sources.transferJustification: Indoor corridor monitoring in a structured facility is the nearest analogue to hall duty; the person-facing part — the substance of monitoring students — is continuously teleoperated, so it cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.system: Tennant autonomous floor-cleaning robots (Spokane Public Schools fleet)
sources.title: Spokane Public Schools Automates Floor Cleaning With Robots | GovTech
sources.claim: Autonomous floor-scrubbing robots are in routine service in US school hallways, but they run after the final bell when students have left, and the work is cleaning rather than supervision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (school corridor floor cleaning) shows that autonomous mobility in school hallways is solved, but the transferred capability is navigation only; it does nothing about student supervision, redirection, or assistance and is scheduled to avoid students entirely.

sources.date: 2016-06 (trials at Singapore public libraries; ongoing use reported since)
sources.title: This Robot Librarian Locates Haphazardly Placed Books | Smithsonian Magazine
sources.claim: The AuRoSS library robot autonomously scans shelves at night using RFID and laser mapping to flag misplaced books; a human librarian must then retrieve and reshelve them, and no student service is provided.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (library inventory shelf-reading) is the closest deployed library robotics; it covers only an audit sub-step and explicitly leaves retrieval, reshelving, circulation, and patron help to human staff, so it cannot complete a library duty period.

sources.system: QUANTUM automatic rear-facing wheelchair securement station
sources.title: Q'STRAINT: QUANTUM Automatic Rear-Facing Wheelchair Securement System
sources.claim: Q'STRAINT QUANTUM is a commercially available automatic wheelchair securement station on buses that secures a chair at the push of a ..., but it requires the passenger to board and position the chair themselves and still involves the driver.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (wheelchair securement) automates one physical sub-step of bus loading. It is a fixed onboard mechanism, not a system that escorts students to the loading zone, matches them to buses, or supervises a dismissal crowd, so it cannot complete the bus-duty instance.

sources.system: Realbotix M-Series humanoid / Optio AI teacher's assistant
sources.title: Realbotix to Deploy First Humanoid Robot and AI Teachers Assistant in U.S. School District
sources.claim: The first announced US school-district humanoid deployment is a conversational classroom assistant pilot, not a mobile supervision or student-assistance system.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to show the state of humanoid robots in US schools as of mid-2026: a stationary conversational unit in a fall-2026 pilot, with no demonstrated hallway, cafeteria, or bus-loop supervision capability.

tasks.label: Sponsor extracurricular activities, such as clubs, student organizations, and academic contests.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Select, store, order, issue, and inventory classroom equipment, materials, and supplies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: During class periods in a resource room or self-contained secondary special-education classroom, the teacher issues instructional materials to individual students: worksheet packets, large-print or braille copies, graphic organizers, manipulatives, calculators, pencil grips, slant boards, AAC devices and school-issued tablets, matching each item to the student's IEP accommodations, setting devices up, swapping out broken or lost items on the spot, then collecting and re-filing everything before the bell. Students are present and moving; the room is cluttered with backpacks, adaptive seating and paraprofessionals.

Selecting and ordering: reviewing vendor catalogs and district-approved curriculum lists, choosing adapted materials and assistive equipment tied to specific IEP goals and to a small annual budget, checking what is already on hand, coordinating with the special-education department chair or AT specialist, entering requisitions in the district purchasing system, and tracking approvals and delivery. Occurs a few times per school year at a desk in the classroom or office.

Receiving and storing: cartons of consumables, class sets of textbooks/workbooks, and boxed assistive devices are dropped at the classroom door; the teacher opens the cartons, checks the packing slip, labels and sorts items into bins and folders, and shelves them in classroom cabinets, a coat-closet storage area, and a locked cabinet for devices, keeping items reachable by students of differing abilities. Heaviest at the start and end ... the school year.

Periodic inventory: counting and reconciling class sets of texts, consumables in bins and drawers, and district-tagged assistive technology (AAC devices, braillers, FM/hearing systems, laptops); checking condition and function, noting damage and missing items, updating the school's inventory or asset-tracking record, and flagging what must be reordered. Items are heterogeneous, partly untagged, and stored in closed cabinets, tubs and drawers. Done once or a few times per year.

Fetching and restocking between rooms: walking to the school's central supply room, workroom or department storeroom to draw paper, folders, toner, laminating film, or a replacement device, signing items out, and transporting them by hand or cart down corridors (sometimes an elevator or a second building) back to the classroom; also returning or exchanging equipment. Happens weekly and as needs arise, usually during passing periods or planning time with students and staff in the halls.

sources.title: Diligent Robotics completes 300,000 pharmacy deliveries with Moxi - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Moxi is an autonomous mobile manipulator deployed in more than 30 US hospitals that fetches supplies from supply closets and delivers them through corridors and elevators to units, without facility modification.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hospital supply fetch-and-delivery. It transfers to a teacher's trip to the school storeroom because both involve retrieving small consumable supplies from a stocked closet in an institutional building and transporting them through staffed corridors and elevators to a specific room.

sources.title: How Diligent's Robots Are Making a Difference in Texas Hospitals - IEEE Spectrum
sources.claim: Moxi performs commercial mobile manipulation, picking supplies ... hospital supply closets and delivering them ... rooms completely autonomously.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: autonomous retrieval of stocked supplies from a closet and delivery to a room in a human-staffed institutional building matches the teacher's storeroom-to-classroom supply run.

sources.title: DHL Supply Chain Achieves First Commercial Deployment of Boston Dynamics' Stretch Robot to Unload Trailers and Containers in the Warehouse
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Stretch robot was commercially deployed by DHL to unload cartons from trailers autonomously, handling mixed stacking without pre-programming.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: carton unloading and induction. It substantiates the receiving half of 'store' when the work is presented to the machine (cartons arriving in a bay/on a conveyor), comparable in object type (mixed cardboard cartons of supplies) though in a purpose-built dock, not a classroom.

sources.title: Amazon robotics: Meet the robots inside fulfillment centers
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm autonomously identifies and moves individual items of many types from containers into specific totes inside fulfillment centers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: piece-picking and sortation of heterogeneous retail goods. It transfers to sorting and binning unpacked classroom consumables (books, folders, boxed devices) when items are presented in totes at a fenced cell, matching object variety and required precision.

sources.title: How Amazon's Vulcan robots use touch to plan and execute motions - Amazon Science
sources.claim: Amazon's Vulcan Stow robots, using force sensing, autonomously stow items into bins on inventory pods and are operating at the Spokane, Washington and Hamburg, Germany ....
sources.transferJustification: Related task: stowing varied items into fabric bins. It substantiates the putaway half of 'store' at E1 — placing heterogeneous small goods into fixed shelf compartments presented to the robot — analogous to filling labeled classroom bins when the shelving is presented as a purpose-built rack.

sources.title: Simbe's Tally Inventory Robot Deployed in Harmons Stores Following Pilot Success
sources.claim: Simbe's Tally autonomously scans shelves in operating grocery stores to capture item-level availability, pricing and placement data, deployed across 17 Harmons stores.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: shelf auditing / stock counting. It transfers to counting classroom stock only where items sit in standardized, tag-labeled locations on open shelving — i.e., when the inventory is presented to the machine — not to closed cabinets and tubs of untagged loose supplies.

sources.title: Autonomous warehouse drones streamline inventory control | TechTarget
sources.claim: Verity's autonomous inventory drones fly warehouse aisles and scan location labels to perform cycle counts, replacing manual counting audits at customer sites and cutting direct inventory costs by half in a documented case.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: physical inventory counting and reconciliation to a records system. It transfers to the counting/recording portion of classroom inventory only when stock is held in labeled, standardized storage locations presented for machine scanning.

roles.description: Provide individualized physical education instruction or services to children, youth, or adults with exceptional physical needs due to gross motor developmental delays or other impairments.

tasks.label: Provide adapted physical education services to students with intellectual disabilities, autism, traumatic brain injury, orthopedic impairments, or other disabling condition.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: One-on-one or small-group motor-skill instruction in a school gym or adapted-PE motor room for ambulatory K-12 students with intellectual disability or autism: set out cones/mats/balls, demonstrate and cue throwing, catching, striking, jumping and locomotor patterns, deliver graduated physical prompts (hand-over-hand, light trunk support), block/redirect elopement and behavior outbursts, keep the student safe, and record IEP progress data.

Session in an APE/motor room for students with orthopedic impairments, cerebral palsy or severe multiple disabilities: transfer the student from wheelchair to mat or stander, don straps/orthoses, provide hands-on support for range of motion, supported standing, assisted stepping and adapted ball or scooter activities, monitor tone, seizures, fatigue and skin, and reposition throughout.

Inclusion support/co-teaching inside a general PE class of 25-30 students: shadow one or two students with disabilities during a fast-moving game or fitness circuit, modify rules and equipment on the fly, give verbal and physical cues, spot for safety amid moving peers and flying balls, and coach peer partners.

Assessment and progress monitoring in the gym: set up test stations, administer gross-motor and fitness assessments (e.g., TGMD-3, Brockport), model each item, give trials, spot/assist students with balance or mobility limits, score performance qualitatively, and document results for the IEP.

Aquatics and community-based APE: in-water instruction at a school or community pool (hands-on flotation support, lifts and pool transfers) and instruction at off-campus sites such as a park trail, bowling alley or community fitness center, with varying layouts, weather and members of the public present.

sources.developer: Aldebaran/SoftBank NAO platform; academic research group (Int. J. Artificial Life Research study)
sources.title: An Autonomous Robot-to-Group Exercise Coach at a Senior Living Community: A Study in Human-Robot Interaction
sources.claim: A NAO humanoid was programmed to autonomously lead a group of elderly residents through seated arm, leg and neck exercises at a senior living community, with nurses/caregivers present; the robot demonstrates and verbally cues but makes no physical contact and provides no hands-on assistance or safety spotting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: leading an exercise routine for a group in a structured facility. It is the closest analogue to APE group instruction, but it covers only non-contact demonstration and verbal cueing for cooperative adults, not the physical prompting, spotting, equipment handling, behavior management and individualized skill correction that APE instances require.

sources.developer: Brest University Hospital / IMT Atlantique / Inria Flowers team
sources.title: Technical Feasibility of Supervision of Stretching Exercises by a Humanoid Robot Coach for Chronic Low Back Pain: The R-COOL Randomized Trial
sources.claim: In a hospital rehabilitation setting, a humanoid robot coach supervised 30-minute daily stretching sessions for adults with chronic low back pain instead of a physiotherapist; the robot only demonstrated and monitored movements, adherence fell over the program and clinicians rated it as not very useful.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-supervised therapeutic exercise, the nearest demonstrated substitution of a robot for a movement professional. Transfer is limited: participants were cognitively intact adults following instructions without physical assistance, and adherence declined, so it does not substantiate delivering an APE session to students who need prompting and hands-on support.

sources.system: Trexo Home / Trexo Plus robotic gait trainer
sources.title: Robot-Assisted Gait Training with Trexo Home: Users, Usage and Initial Impacts
sources.claim: The Trexo Home/Plus pediatric lower-limb exoskeleton mounted on a wheeled ... delivers repetitive powered stepping for children with cerebral palsy at home, school and clinics, but an adult must fit and strap the child in, set parameters, steer the frame and supervise the session.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-assisted gait training for children with severe mobility impairment, overlapping the orthopedic-impairment APE instance. It is a caregiver-operated powered device executing a preset gait pattern; the human still performs the transfer, donning, steering and all instruction, so it does not complete the instance.

sources.system: RISTA (Robot-mediated Imitation Skill Training Architecture, NAO-based)
sources.title: Robot-Mediated Imitation Skill Training for Children With Autism
sources.claim: Robot-mediated imitation skill training for children with autism has been implemented with a humanoid robot able to run sessions autonomously, but the training is limited to seated gesture/pose imitation in a controlled lab room with an adult present.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led motor imitation training for children with autism, a component skill of APE instruction. Transfer is partial only: it addresses small seated gestures with no equipment, no physical prompting, no safety supervision and no whole-body gross-motor skills.

sources.system: Realbotix M-Series humanoid with Optio AI teaching assistant
sources.title: US firm to deploy humanoid robot teaching assistant in New York schools
sources.claim: Humanoid robots entering US K-12 schools in 2026 are deployed as conversational AI teaching assistants and tutors for academic content, not as providers of physical instruction or hands-on student support.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic teaching assistance in a school. It establishes the current school-deployment frontier is stationary conversational tutoring, which does not carry over to adapted physical education requiring movement instruction, physical prompting and safety management.

tasks.label: Provide students positive feedback to encourage them and help them develop an appreciation for physical education.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Provide individual or small groups of students with adapted physical education instruction that meets desired physical needs or goals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: One-on-one session in a school gym, motor room or therapy space with a student who has significant physical impairment (cerebral palsy, spina bifida, low tone, wheelchair user): the specialist positions or transfers the student, provides manual support/spotting and hand-over-hand guidance, sets up adapted equipment (mats, ramps, switch-activated devices, therapy balls), runs stretching, strength, mobility and skill practice toward IEP goals, and records progress.

Small group (2-5 students) with autism, intellectual disability or behavioral needs in a school gym or multipurpose room: the specialist sets up and rotates stations, demonstrates and physically prompts throwing, catching, kicking, striking, balance and locomotor skills, hands out and retrieves balls/scooters/beanbags, redirects off-task or eloping students, and adapts activities in real time.

Push-in / inclusion support inside a general physical education class: the specialist works alongside the PE teacher with one or two students on the class activity, modifying rules and equipment, cueing and physically assisting the student, arranging peer partners, and keeping the student safe within a moving class of 25-30 children.

Preschool / early-childhood gross motor session in a motor room or classroom with a child with developmental delay: play-based obstacle courses, climbing, jumping, ball play and sensorimotor activities, with the specialist physically supporting, lifting, guiding and motivating the child and reconfiguring soft equipment between activities.

Session in an aquatic, outdoor or community setting (school or community pool, playground, track, community fitness center): the specialist provides in-water support or supervision, guides the student over uneven or shared public surfaces, uses whatever equipment the site offers, and manages safety among other users and variable weather.

sources.developer: Universidad Carlos III de Madrid / Universidad de Málaga, with Hospital Virgen del Rocío (Seville)
sources.title: Evaluating the Child–Robot Interaction of the NAOTherapist Platform in Pediatric Rehabilitation
sources.claim: NAOTherapist runs autonomous, explicitly non-contact upper-limb rehabilitation sessions with children with physical impairments in a hospital rehabilitation setting; the robot demonstrates poses and monitors the patient but never touches or supports them.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led individualized therapeutic exercise sessions for children with motor impairment, the closest analogue to adapted PE instruction. It shows what autonomous systems can do (verbal/gestural exercise leading) and what they cannot (any physical contact, equipment handling, or safety support), which is the decisive limit for this task.

sources.developer: University of Toronto (Autonomous Systems and Biomechatronics Lab)
sources.title: Long-Term Exercise Assistance: Group and One-on-One Interactions between a Social Robot and Seniors
sources.claim: A Pepper robot autonomously led nine upper-body exercises with older adults in both group and one-on-one sessions during a long-term study in a residential care facility.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led small-group and individual exercise instruction inside an institutional facility. It is the strongest evidence for autonomous exercise leading in an E2 setting, but the exercises are seated, hands-off upper-body movements with cooperative adults, with no equipment handling, prompting hierarchy, or safety supervision of children.

sources.date: 2013 (journal), on-site sessions at a senior living community
sources.title: An Autonomous Robot-to-Group Exercise Coach at a Senior Living Community: A Study in Human-Robot Interaction
sources.claim: A NAO humanoid acted as an autonomous exercise instructor for seniors at a senior living community, leading warm-up and exercise routines with vision-based monitoring.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous group exercise instruction in a human-occupied institutional facility. Establishes the ceiling of demonstrated capability — verbal/gestural coaching of simple movements — without any of the physical assistance, equipment setup, or child safety management adapted PE requires.

sources.system: Humanoid robot therapeutic assistant for arm rehabilitation
sources.developer: Reported in Frontiers in Robotics and AI (clinical study)
sources.title: Analysis of the therapeutic interaction provided by a humanoid robot serving stroke survivors as a therapeutic assistant for arm rehabilitation
sources.claim: In a controlled trial of humanoid-robot-led arm rehabilitation for stroke survivors, the robot could act only as a social agent, providing no physical assistance, and every robot-led session had supervising staff present for safety.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led therapeutic movement sessions. Directly documents that current humanoid session leaders provide no manual assistance and require human staff on hand for safety, which rules out completion of adapted PE instances that depend on manual support and supervision.

sources.system: Clinical robot-assisted therapy platforms (survey of deployed devices, e.g., arm/hand trainers)
sources.developer: ETH Zurich / University Hospital Zurich (design and pilot usability study)
sources.title: Towards a platform for robot-assisted minimally-supervised therapy of hand function: design and pilot usability evaluation
sources.claim: Robot-assisted therapy with hands-on devices (e.g., end-effector and exoskeleton trainers) still requires a supervising therapist to prepare the equipment, set the patient up in the device and configure the therapy plan for each session.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: physically contacting rehabilitation robots (the only machines that move a person's limbs). Shows that even in purpose-built settings these devices are clinician-operated tools, not autonomous providers of a whole instructional session, so an E1 'work brought to the machine' route is not substantiated.

sources.developer: Maastricht University / Adelante rehabilitation (Van den Heuvel et al.), reviewed in Bioengineering
sources.title: Exploring the Impact of Socially Assistive Robots in Rehabilitation Scenarios
sources.claim: ZORA robot interventions with children with severe physical disabilities in rehabilitation and special education were tablet-operated imitation sessions run by professionals, with engagement declining as novelty wore off.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot sessions with the exact student population of adapted PE (children with severe physical disabilities, individual and group). Operation is by a professional via tablet and the robot never handles equipment or the child, so it cannot substantiate autonomous completion.

sources.developer: Oregon State University (Fitter, Logan et al.)
sources.date: 2024-10 journal article; 2025-02 study coverage; RA-L 2025 children with motor disabilities
sources.title: Toddlers show increased physical activity with a robot playmate moving around the room
sources.claim: GoBot, an autonomous wheeled assistive robot, encouraged movement practice by toddlers, including children with motor disabilities, in individual playroom sessions; it elicits activity but delivers no instruction, physical support, or equipment handling.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: eliciting gross-motor activity from young children with developmental delay, the population of early-childhood adapted PE. It shows autonomous movement elicitation in a controlled playroom, but not goal-directed instruction, manual guidance, or session management.

tasks.label: Instruct students, using adapted physical education techniques, to improve physical fitness, gross motor skills, perceptual motor skills, or sports and game achievement.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-group adapted PE class (3-8 students) in a school gymnasium or multipurpose room: elementary/middle students with autism, intellectual disability, ADHD or developmental delay. Specialist sets up stations (cones, mats, scooters, balls), demonstrates skills, gives verbal/visual/physical prompts, redirects behavior, keeps students safe, and records IEP progress data.

One-to-one session with a student with a severe physical impairment (cerebral palsy GMFCS III-V, wheelchair user) in a school gym or motor room: positioning and transfers, supported standing/walking, hand-over-hand assistance with striking, rolling and throwing, range-of-motion work, switch-activated or adapted equipment.

Inclusion support in general PE: specialist supports 1-3 students with disabilities inside a class of ~25 in the gym or on an outdoor field, modifying drills and game rules in real time, cueing peers, physically guiding the student through sport skills, and watching for safety in fast-moving play.

Community-based instruction: adapted aquatics at a school or community pool (in-water physical support, flotation, teaching stroke and water-safety skills) or a bowling alley / community fitness outing teaching leisure-sport skills.

Individual fitness/conditioning session in a school fitness room: student with a mild-to-moderate disability works through a prescribed circuit (calisthenics, resistance bands, stationary bike, rep-counted exercises) while the specialist demonstrates each movement, cues form, counts repetitions, motivates, and monitors exertion.

Itinerant home- or community-based session (early intervention or transition-age adult): gross-motor play and fitness activities in a family living room, daycare room, or neighborhood playground, with improvised equipment, family or caregivers present, and a layout that differs at every visit.

sources.developer: Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (Krakovsky et al.)
sources.title: "Gymmy": Designing and Testing a Robot for Physical and Cognitive Training of Older Adults
sources.claim: Gymmy is a humanoid robotic exercise trainer that autonomously demonstrates exercises, measures the user's performance with an RGB-D camera and skeleton tracking, and gives spoken feedback; tested with 26 older adults performing training sessions in home settings.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: coaching a client through a prescribed exercise routine. It transfers to the fitness-conditioning slice of adapted PE because the instructional acts are the same (demonstrate the movement, cue form, count repetitions, give corrective feedback) and no handling of the client or of equipment is required; the exercises are body-weight movements at a single fixed station.

sources.developer: Universidad de Extremadura / Virgen del Rocío University Hospital
sources.title: A gamified social robotics platform for intensive therapies in neurorehabilitation
sources.claim: NAOTherapist is a socially assistive robot platform that autonomously runs gamified upper-limb rehabilitation sessions for pediatric cerebral palsy patients; it is explicitly hands-off (no physical contact) and was deployed at a university hospital for a long-term adherence study.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: pediatric motor rehabilitation exercise sessions with children who have the same impairments as adapted PE students. It shows the reachable envelope — pose-imitation exercise coaching with no physical contact — and therefore cannot substantiate the hands-on, equipment-based, multi-student parts of adapted PE instruction.

sources.title: Teaching imitation to children with autism, by QTrobot for autism
sources.claim: QTrobot is a commercially sold social robot used by schools, clinics and families for special-needs education; its curricula practice gross-motor imitation, and sessions are designed to run with the human trainer actively involved.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: teaching gross-motor imitation to children with autism in special-education settings. It is the closest deployed classroom system to adapted PE instruction, but it is a stationary tabletop social robot operated as an adjunct alongside a trainer, so it cannot substantiate independent completion of an adapted PE session.

sources.system: Socially assistive robots in physiotherapy (review of multiple platforms)
sources.title: Use of Socially Assistive Robots in Physiotherapy: Scoping Review
sources.claim: A 2025 scoping review of socially assistive robots in physiotherapy finds that these robots occupy coaching, demonstration, monitoring and peer-support roles in interventions — i.e., non-contact adjunct roles rather than delivering hands-on therapy.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: physiotherapy exercise delivery, which shares the population and movement goals of adapted PE. The review establishes that current robots in this field coach and demonstrate rather than physically assist, bounding what can be credited for hands-on instructional instances.

sources.title: Physiotherapy-assisted overground exoskeleton use: mixed methods feasibility study protocol ... in children with mobility impairments
sources.claim: Trexo Plus is a commercially available pediatric lower-limb exoskeleton on a wheeled walker that powers a child's leg movements for gait training; it is fitted to the child and operated/adjusted by a therapist or parent via a tablet.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hands-on gross-motor (gait) training for children with cerebral palsy, the same population as adapted PE. It is the main physically contacting robot in this domain, but the child must be transferred and strapped in and the device is tablet-driven and supervised, so it cannot support an autonomous-completion judgment.

sources.title: Google AI robot beats humans at table tennis, wins 45% of matches
sources.claim: DeepMind's table tennis robot plays autonomous rallies and full matches against human players at an intermediate amateur level on a purpose-built instrumented table setup.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: playing a sport with a human partner. It shows autonomous sport interaction exists only as a single-sport, fixtured table setup with a cooperative able-bodied opponent; it provides no instruction, adaptation of equipment or rules, prompting, or safety supervision, so it does not transfer to adapted PE instruction.

tasks.label: Write reports to summarize student performance, social growth, or physical development.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Evaluate the motor needs of individual students to determine their need for adapted physical education services.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Formal initial eligibility evaluation of an elementary student with a developmental delay or autism: the specialist reserves the school gym/multipurpose room, gathers and sets up equipment (marks lines 15 ft apart, cones, balls, bat/tee), administers a standardized gross motor battery (TGMD-3 or BOT-2) by demonstrating each skill, tossing balls underhand for catching items, retrieving equipment, redirecting and re-prompting an inattentive child, scoring each performance criterion, then combines results with record review and teacher interview into an eligibility report.

Screening/observation of a referred student during regular PE class or recess: the specialist watches the student in the gym or on the playground against a checklist/rubric, may pull the student aside for a few informal motor probes with a ball or jump rope, consults the PE teacher and classroom staff, and decides whether a full evaluation or services are warranted.

Evaluation of a student with a significant physical disability (e.g., cerebral palsy, wheelchair user, multiple disabilities): functional/ecological assessment in the gym or therapy room requiring hands-on positioning and support, transfers with an aide, checking range of motion and postural control, trialing adapted equipment (switch-activated devices, walker, adapted bat), and determining how much physical prompting/assistance the student needs, coordinated with PT/OT.

Triennial re-evaluation of a student already receiving adapted PE: re-administer selected test items and curriculum-based/rubric measures during instruction in the gym, collect progress data against IEP goals, and write the continuing-need determination.

Early-childhood or community-based evaluation conducted outside a standard school gym — a preschool play space, a family home, or a community rec center — with a parent or caregiver present, using play-based motor assessment in whatever space and equipment is available.

Secondary/transition-age student assessment of health-related fitness and functional motor skills (e.g., Brockport Physical Fitness Test) in the gym, weight room, or track: setting up and running PACER/aerobic items, strength and flexibility items requiring equipment handling and spotting, and interpreting results for adapted PE need.

sources.developer: BKIN Technologies / University of Calgary (Kirton lab)
sources.title: Stimulation for Perinatal Stroke Optimizing Recovery Trajectories (NCT03216837)
sources.claim: The KINARM robotic exoskeleton, adapted for children, administers standardized sensorimotor tasks (position matching, kinesthesia, visually guided reaching) and yields objective measures of motor impairment in children with hemiparetic cerebral palsy, in a clinic/lab setting with the child seated and fixtured in the device.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: instrumented robotic assessment of children's motor function. It does NOT transfer to this task: KINARM measures seated upper-limb reaching/kinesthesia inside a purpose-built rig, whereas adapted PE evaluation requires eliciting and judging whole-body gross motor skills (run, hop, skip, throw, catch, kick), adapting the protocol and equipment to the child, ensuring safety, and integrating observation, records and interviews into a services-eligibility determination. Setup, seating and fitting of the child are performed by a technician.

sources.system: Gymmy robotic physical-training coach (Poppy/NAO-class humanoid + RGB-D camera)
sources.developer: Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (Krakovsky et al.)
sources.title: Robotic System for Physical Training of Older Adults — International Journal of Social Robotics
sources.claim: The 'Gymmy' robotic trainer physically demonstrates exercises and, via an attached RGB-D camera, monitors and evaluates a user's movement performance during training sessions; demonstrated in lab studies with older adults.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led exercise with automated movement monitoring. It does not transfer: Gymmy prompts pre-programmed seated/standing exercises for cooperative adults in a lab room and gives simple feedback; it does not set up test courses, toss balls, physically support or prompt a child with disabilities, select or adapt an assessment battery, or produce a defensible eligibility determination.

sources.developer: reported in Perceptual and Motor Skills (Guo, Zhang & Zhang)
sources.title: AI-Powered Assessment of Motor Development: Using Platforms Like KineticAI to Analyze Fundamental Movement Skills in Children
sources.claim: Automated analysis of children's fundamental movement skills has been studied using camera/AI platforms (e.g., KineticAI) compared with human raters in school children, but such platforms are software-and-sensor systems with no physical embodiment acting on the world.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated scoring of children's fundamental movement skills. It cannot support a positive judgment because it is software-only (vision/AI scoring), not a physically embodied robotic system: a human still sets up the course, elicits and tosses to the child, manages safety, and writes the determination.

tasks.label: Collaborate with other educational personnel to provide inclusive activities or programs for children with disabilities.

tasks.label: Adapt instructional techniques to the age and skill levels of students.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Elementary school gym, small-group or inclusive APE session with students who have autism or developmental delay: mid-lesson the specialist recognizes the throwing drill is too complex, re-sequences it into a shorter task-analytic progression, swaps a verbal cue for a picture card or peer model, and slows pacing to match the group's skill level.

One-to-one session with a student with a significant physical impairment (e.g., cerebral palsy, wheelchair user): the specialist selects and shifts prompt level (least-to-most), changes the success criterion, shortens distances or repetitions, and re-explains the movement in simpler terms so the instruction matches the student's current motor ability.

Secondary-school student (ages 12-21): the specialist re-frames instruction to be chronologically age-appropriate rather than childish, using fitness-center/lifetime-sport framing, self-monitoring checklists, and peer tutoring, while keeping the skill demands at the student's actual performance level.

Preschool / early-childhood or early-intervention setting (ages 3-5): the specialist converts the movement objective into short, play-based, imitation-driven instructional formats with very simple language, brief attention windows, and songs or games suited to developmental age.

Off-the-floor planning and consultation: writing lesson plans and IEP-aligned instructional strategies, and coaching the general PE teacher or paraprofessional on which cueing, prompting, and progression to use for a given student's age and skill level.

tasks.label: Assist in screening or placement of students in adapted physical education programs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Administering a standardized gross-motor assessment (e.g., TGMD-3, BOT-2, Peabody) to an elementary student referred for APE evaluation in the school gym: setting out cones, mats, balls and a batting tee, demonstrating each skill, tossing balls for catching trials, spotting for safety, watching multiple trials and scoring each performance criterion on the protocol.

Informal screening/observation of a referred student during their regular general PE class or recess: handing out equipment, running short informal skill trials, comparing the student with peers on a checklist, and consulting the PE teacher — school gym, playground or multipurpose room.

Hands-on screening of a student with significant physical or multiple disabilities in a therapy room or adapted gym: transferring/positioning the student out of a wheelchair, providing physical support and hand-over-hand prompting, trying adaptive equipment (switch-activated devices, supported standers, modified balls) to determine what the student can do.

School- or district-wide motor screening event with several stations in a gym: multiple students rotating through hopping, running, throwing and balance items, quick scoring, crowd and safety supervision, flagging students for full evaluation.

Contributing to the placement decision: writing the assessment report, presenting findings at an eligibility/IEP meeting in a school conference room, and recommending service level (general PE with supports, small-group APE, or one-to-one APE).

sources.system: Socially assistive child-robot exercise coaching system (NAO-class humanoid)
sources.title: Socially assistive child-robot interaction in physical exercise coaching | IEEE Conference Publication
sources.claim: An autonomous socially assistive robot can lead children through a set of physical exercise motions with real-time feedback — the closest robot capability to eliciting motor performance from a child — but it coaches prescribed motions rather than administering, scoring and interpreting a standardized motor assessment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led physical exercise sessions with children. It shows a robot can prompt and give feedback on gross motor movement, but there is no evidence it sets up test equipment, tosses balls, spots students, or scores standardized motor items for eligibility decisions, so it does not carry over to whole-instance screening.

sources.title: Test–retest reliability of KINARM robot sensorimotor and cognitive assessment: in pediatric ice hockey players - PMC
sources.claim: A commercial robotic device (Kinarm exoskeleton) administers standardized, automated upper-limb sensorimotor and cognitive test batteries with quantitative scoring in a purpose-built laboratory setting, including with pediatric subjects.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic quantitative assessment of motor function. Transfer fails for APE screening because the device measures seated upper-limb reaching in a fixtured exoskeleton, not whole-body locomotor and object-control skills (running, hopping, catching, striking) in a gym, and it produces research metrics rather than an educational eligibility/placement determination.

sources.system: SoftBank Pepper (school deployment reported in CARE review)
sources.title: CARE: towards customized assistive robot-based education - PMC
sources.claim: Humanoid social robots have been operated autonomously inside schools for student interaction and wellbeing support, establishing that school premises are a feasible robot environment, but the reported role is conversational/social support rather than motor screening or placement.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous social robot operation in a school. It substantiates only presence and social interaction in an E2 school setting; no evidence of administering motor tests, handling test equipment, physically supporting students, or contributing scored assessment data.

tasks.label: Assess students' physical progress or needs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Administering a standardized motor-development battery (TGMD-3, BOT-2, PDMS-2) to an individual student in a school gym or multipurpose room: setting out cones/balls/mats, demonstrating each skill, tossing or rolling balls for catch/strike items, giving practice and scored trials, judging qualitative performance criteria trial by trial, keeping the child engaged and safe, then recording raw scores.

Ongoing progress monitoring of IEP motor goals during an adapted or general PE class: observing the student in activity, running short probes (e.g., number of successful throws, laps, transitions), scoring rubrics/checklists, comparing to baseline data, in a gym or playground with other students, equipment and noise present.

Physical fitness testing with adaptations (Brockport/FitnessGram): PACER or timed run with a pacing cue, grip dynamometer, back-saver sit-and-reach, curl-ups/trunk lift, wheelchair-adapted items; setting up, timing, counting, spotting, motivating, and comparing results to criterion standards, in a school gym or track.

Assessing a student with severe or multiple disabilities (wheelchair user, cerebral palsy, medically fragile) in a therapy room, classroom or adapted PE space: hands-on positioning and transfers, passive range-of-motion and tone/strength screening, functional mobility and adapted-skill probes, often with a paraeducator assisting, then determining present levels and needs.

Assessment in an unstructured setting: early-intervention home visit, preschool play space, community park/playground, or community fitness center for transition assessment; layout and equipment differ site to site, family members or the public are present, and the specialist improvises test items and adaptations.

sources.title: Non-Linear Modeling of Motor Development in Typically Developing Children and Youth Aged 5–18 Years Using Robot-Based Behavioral Assessments
sources.claim: The Kinarm Exoskeleton robot administers standardized seated upper-limb tasks (point-to-point reaching, object hitting) to children aged 5-18 and computes performance parameters against normative models; it is a laboratory/clinical research device covering only the movements executable inside the robot, with researchers positioning and instructing participants.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-administered quantitative motor assessment of children. It is the closest robotic analogue to 'assess students' physical progress', but covers only seated upper-limb kinematics inside a fixturing exoskeleton, not gross-motor skill batteries, fitness items, or needs determination, so it does not transfer to whole-instance completion.

sources.title: Software - Hocoma (Lokomat)
sources.claim: The Lokomat gait-training exoskeleton includes robotic assessment tools (L-ROM, L-FORCE, L-STIFF) that measure hip/knee range of motion, isometric force and stiffness while the patient is strapped into the device in a rehabilitation clinic; a therapist sets up, secures and supervises the patient and interprets the output.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic measurement of joint range of motion and strength, a component of assessing a student's physical needs. Transfer is limited: the device measures only hip/knee parameters of a strapped-in patient and produces no functional-skill judgment, so it cannot deliver the accepted output of an adapted PE assessment.

sources.developer: Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (Edan et al.)
sources.title: “Gymmy”: Designing and Testing a Robot for Physical and Cognitive Training of Older Adults
sources.claim: The 'Gymmy' robotic trainer demonstrates exercises and uses an RGB-D camera to measure a user's exercise performance and give feedback; it was tested as a research prototype with 26 older adults in home environments, monitoring prescribed repetitions rather than administering a standardized motor assessment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led supervision and measurement of a person's movement performance. It shows the frontier of autonomous movement scoring by a robot, but is limited to cooperative adults performing prescribed exercises in front of a fixed camera, not criterion-scored gross-motor testing of children with disabilities.

sources.system: Socially assistive robots in physiotherapy (review of multiple systems)
sources.developer: multiple (review by JMIR Rehabilitation and Assistive Technologies authors)
sources.title: Use of Socially Assistive Robots in Physiotherapy: Scoping Review
sources.claim: A 2025 scoping review of socially assistive robots in physiotherapy finds the clinical literature is still limited by small sample sizes and technical issues in robot and intervention design, indicating research-stage rather than deployed capability for robot-led movement therapy and monitoring.
sources.transferJustification: Related field: robot-delivered physical therapy coaching and monitoring, the nearest professional analogue to adapted PE assessment. The review establishes that such systems remain at clinical-study stage, supporting negative judgments about worker-quality assessment delivery.

sources.title: Nao: A Promising Tool for Pediatric Hospitals
sources.claim: Child-facing humanoid robot sessions that involve body-movement tasks (e.g., imitation of body patterns) in a pediatric hospital are run by Wizard-of-Oz teleoperation, with an experimenter controlling the NAO robot out of sight.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-administered movement tasks with children. It shows that even simple child movement-imitation protocols are typically human-driven, so no autonomous robot administration of motor test items with children is substantiated.
